subtopics.title: CPU Structure, ALU & Control Unit
subtopics.subtitle: Registers, ALU, instruction cycle in RTL, Mano's basic computer and how control is built

concepts.text: What the CPU Contains

The central processing unit executes the instructions of a program. It fetches each instruction from memory, decodes it, and carries out the operation on data held in registers or memory. Three functional parts are always present: an arithmetic logic unit that performs the data processing, a register set that holds operands, addresses and status, and a control unit that generates the timing and control signals which steer everything. They talk to each other over an internal bus and to memory and I/O over the external system bus.
The four building blocks of a CPU and what each does:
items: Arithmetic Logic Unit (ALU): combinational circuit that performs add, subtract, AND, OR, XOR, complement, shift and compare on operands supplied from the registers.
Register set: a small, very fast storage array inside the processor; holds the next-instruction address, the current instruction, operands, intermediate results and the status flags.
Control unit: decodes the opcode in the instruction register and, using a timing generator, issues the sequence of control signals that move data between registers, the ALU and memory.
Internal (CPU) bus: the common path over which register contents are routed to the ALU and back; a bus with 2^k sources needs k select lines.

concepts.text: Arithmetic and Logic Unit

The ALU is a combinational circuit with two n-bit data inputs, a function-select input from the control unit, and an n-bit output plus status bits. The arithmetic section is built from an n-bit parallel adder; adding a control line M that complements the second operand and injects a carry-in of 1 turns the same adder into a subtractor (A − B = A + B' + 1 in 2's complement). The logic section computes AND, OR, XOR and NOT bit by bit, and a shifter provides logical, arithmetic and circular shifts. After every operation the flags are updated: Z if the result is all zeros, S from the most significant bit, C from the final carry-out, and V when the carries into and out of the sign position differ.
A one-bit adder/subtractor cell, repeated n times, is the core of the arithmetic section:
items: Full adder: sum S = A XOR B XOR Cin; carry-out Cout = AB + Cin(A XOR B). Chaining n cells with ripple carry gives an n-bit adder.
Subtractor: feed B through an XOR gate with the mode line M. With M = 0 the cell adds; with M = 1 it adds the complement of B and, with the initial carry set to 1, computes A − B.
Overflow in signed arithmetic is detected as V = Cn XOR Cn−1, the XOR of the carry into and out of the sign bit.
Multiplication and division are usually done by repeated add-and-shift sequences under control-unit supervision rather than by a single ALU function.

concepts.text: Instruction Cycle and Register Transfer Language

Every instruction passes through the same cycle: fetch (read the instruction word at the address in PC into IR and advance PC), decode (the control unit examines the opcode and mode bits, and computes the effective address if the operand is in memory), execute (perform the micro-operations the instruction requires), and finally an interrupt check (if interrupts are enabled and one is pending, save PC and jump to the service routine). Register transfer language (RTL) describes each step as a micro-operation, an elementary transfer that happens in one clock pulse, written as destination ← source with an optional control condition in front of a colon.
The fetch and decode phases of Mano's basic computer written in RTL (T0, T1, T2 are timing signals):
items: T0: AR ← PC. The address of the next instruction is moved to the address register.
T1: IR ← M[AR], PC ← PC + 1. The instruction word is read into IR while PC is incremented in the same clock pulse.
T2: D0…D7 ← Decode IR(12–14), AR ← IR(0–11), I ← IR(15). The opcode is decoded, the address field goes to AR and the mode bit to flip-flop I.
D7'IT3: AR ← M[AR]. If the instruction is memory-reference and indirect (I = 1), one more read fetches the effective address.
Four classes of micro-operation appear in RTL: register transfer (R1 ← R2), arithmetic (R1 ← R1 + R2), logic (R1 ← R1 XOR R2) and shift (R1 ← shl R1).

concepts.text: Computer Configuration: Mano's Basic Computer
Morris Mano's basic computer is the standard reference configuration for the syllabus:
items: Memory: 4096 words of 16 bits (4096 × 16), so an address is 12 bits and one word holds an instruction or a data item.

Instruction format: bit 15 is the mode bit I (0 direct, 1 indirect), bits 12–14 are the opcode, bits 0–11 are the address. Opcodes 000–110 are memory-reference (AND, ADD, LDA, STA, BUN, BSA, ISZ); opcode 111 with I = 0 is register-reference and with I = 1 is input-output.
Registers: AR 12 bits, PC 12 bits, DR 16, AC 16, IR 16, TR 16 (temporary), OUTR 8 and INPR 8 for the output and input devices.
Flip-flops: I (indirect), S (start/stop), E (carry out of AC), R (interrupt), IEN (interrupt enable), FGI and FGO (input and output flags).
Common bus: one 16-bit bus with three select lines S2 S1 S0 chooses among 8 sources (000 none, 001 AR, 010 PC, 011 DR, 100 AC, 101 IR, 110 TR, 111 memory); each register has an LD, INR and CLR input.

concepts.text: Timing and control signals come from a 4-bit sequence counter SC whose output drives a 4 × 16 decoder producing timing signals T0 to T15; a 3 × 8 decoder on IR(12–14) produces the opcode signals D0 to D7. A control function is a Boolean product of these, for example the BUN instruction executes as D4T4: PC ← AR, SC ← 0, and the last micro-operation of every instruction clears SC so that the next fetch starts at T0. The control unit's design problem is to generate every LD, INR, CLR, bus-select and memory read/write signal as a Boolean function of the D, T, I and flag variables. There are two ways to realise those Boolean functions. A hardwired control unit implements them directly with gates, decoders and flip-flops, so a change in the instruction set means rewiring the circuit; it is fast and is the choice for RISC processors. A microprogrammed control unit stores the control signals for each step as words in a control memory, and a sequencer reads them out one after another; it is slower but flexible and is the traditional CISC approach. The next subtopic develops the microprogrammed design in detail.

Slower; one control-memory read per micro-step

concepts.text: Going Deeper: Datapath, Hardwired Control and Stacks

A common bus for k registers of n bits can be built in two ways. With multiplexers, bit i of every register goes to multiplexer i, so the bus needs n multiplexers of size k × 1 that share ceil(log2 k) select lines. With three-state buffers, every register bit gets its own buffer (k × n buffers) and a log2 k × k decoder enables exactly one register at a time, because two drivers on one bus line would conflict. Either way only one source can use the bus in a clock, but paths that bypass the bus still work in parallel: in Mano's basic computer AC ← DR (through the adder and logic circuit) can happen in the same clock as DR ← AC (over the bus), and the INR and CLR inputs change a register without using the bus at all.

concepts.text: Mano's arithmetic circuit computes D = A + Y + Cin (table above); logic micro-operations manipulate bits and shifts move them sideways:
items: Selective set A ← A ∨ B sets the bits of A where B has 1s; selective complement A ← A ⊕ B inverts them; selective clear A ← A ∧ B' clears them.

Mask A ← A ∧ B keeps the bits of A only where B has 1s; insert first masks the target bits to 0 and then ORs in the new pattern; the clear (compare) operation A ← A ⊕ B gives all 0s exactly when A and B are equal.
Example with A = 1001 0110 and B = 0000 1111: selective set gives 1001 1111, selective complement 1001 1001, selective clear 1001 0000 and mask 0000 0110.

Logical shifts insert 0 and circular shifts feed the bit that falls out back into the other end. Arithmetic shift right copies the sign bit (a signed divide by 2); arithmetic shift left multiplies by 2 and overflows when R(n−1) and R(n−2) differ before the shift, Vs = R(n−1) ⊕ R(n−2).

concepts.text:
Worked example 1: clock cycles in Mano's basic computer, 100 ns clock (10 MHz)
Every instruction: T0-T2 fetch and decode, T3 indirect check
LDA X (I = 1) : D2T4 DR <- M[AR]; D2T5 AC <- DR, SC <- 0      T0..T5 = 6
ADD Y (I = 0) : D1T4 DR <- M[AR]; D1T5 AC <- AC + DR           T0..T5 = 6
ISZ C         : D6T4 read; D6T5 DR <- DR + 1; D6T6 write, skip  T0..T6 = 7
BUN L         : D4T4 PC <- AR, SC <- 0                         T0..T4 = 5
CMA (reg-ref) : D7 I' T3 B9: AC <- AC'                          T0..T3 = 4
Total = 6 + 6 + 7 + 5 + 4 = 28 cycles
Time  = 28 x 100 ns = 2.8 µs
I = 1 costs no extra cycle: every memory-reference instruction spends T3 anyway

Designing a hardwired control unit is careful bookkeeping. List every micro-operation that changes a register, note the control function (decoder output D, timing signal T, mode bit I, flags) under which it occurs, and OR those functions to drive that register's LD, INR or CLR input. For Mano's PC, PC ← AR occurs in BUN (D4T4) and BSA (D5T5), so LD(PC) = D4T4 + D5T5, while PC ← 0 in the interrupt cycle gives CLR(PC) = RT1. The timing signals come from a binary counter plus decoder (log2 k flip-flops for k signals), a ring counter (k flip-flops, no decoder) or a Johnson counter (k/2 flip-flops, each state decoded by a 2-input AND gate), and only as many signals are needed as the longest instruction uses.
Mano's interrupt cycle replaces the next fetch when flip-flop R is 1:
items: R is set by T0'T1'T2'(IEN)(FGI + FGO): R ← 1, that is outside the fetch and decode steps, with interrupts enabled and a device flag raised.
RT0: AR ← 0, TR ← PC. The return address is parked in TR while AR is cleared.
RT1: M[AR] ← TR, PC ← 0. The return address is stored in memory word 0.
RT2: PC ← PC + 1, IEN ← 0, R ← 0, SC ← 0. The next fetch comes from word 1, which holds a BUN to the service routine; IEN stays 0 until the routine executes ION.
The service routine ends with an indirect BUN 0, which jumps back through the address saved in word 0.

concepts.text: A stack is either a set of fast registers or a region of main memory, addressed by the stack pointer SP. Mano's 64-word register stack has a 6-bit SP and flags FULL and EMTY: PUSH is SP ← SP + 1, M[SP] ← DR (FULL ← 1 if SP has wrapped to 0, EMTY ← 0), and POP is DR ← M[SP], SP ← SP − 1 (EMTY ← 1 if SP = 0, FULL ← 0). Because SP is incremented before the write, the first item goes into word 1 and the 64th wraps into word 0. A memory stack usually grows toward lower addresses (PUSH: SP ← SP − 1, M[SP] ← DR; POP: DR ← M[SP], SP ← SP + 1), and limit registers compared with SP catch overflow and underflow. Stack machines evaluate expressions in reverse Polish notation, so zero-address instructions find their operands on the top of the stack.

concepts.text: Common slips: the number of bus multiplexers equals the word length, not the number of registers; an arithmetic shift right copies the sign bit while a logical shift inserts 0; in postfix evaluation the item popped first is the right operand of − and /; whether SP changes before or after the write depends on whether it points to the top item or to the next free word; and in Mano's timing an indirect memory-reference instruction takes no more clock cycles than a direct one.

notes.text: Memorise the numbers of Mano's basic computer: 16-bit word, 4096 × 16 memory, 12-bit address, 3-bit opcode plus 1 mode bit, 8 registers (AR PC DR AC IR TR OUTR INPR), 3 bus select lines. MCQs often ask for one of these figures directly.

MAR and MBR (AR and DR in Mano's notation) sit between the CPU and memory: MAR carries an address out, MBR carries data in or out. Do not confuse MBR with the accumulator, which is an ALU operand register.
In RTL, all micro-operations listed on one line with a common control function happen in the same clock pulse, e.g. T1: IR ← M[AR], PC ← PC + 1 reads memory and increments PC simultaneously.

questions.questionText: Mano's basic computer has a memory of 4096 words of 16 bits. How many bits are used for the address field and for the opcode field (excluding the mode bit) of an instruction?
questions.explanation: 4096 = 2^12 words need a 12-bit address (bits 0–11). Bits 12–14 form the 3-bit opcode and bit 15 is the indirect mode bit I, filling the 16-bit word.

questions.questionText: Which register-transfer sequence correctly describes the fetch phase of a basic computer?
options: T0: IR ← M[PC]; T1: PC ← PC + 1; T2: AR ← IR
T0: AR ← IR; T1: PC ← M[AR]; T2: IR ← PC
T0: AR ← PC; T1: IR ← M[AR], PC ← PC + 1
T0: DR ← M[PC]; T1: AC ← DR; T2: PC ← PC + 1
questions.explanation: The address in PC is first transferred to AR (memory is addressed only through AR), then the word is read into IR while PC is incremented in the same clock pulse.

questions.questionText: In the standard CPU organisation described by Mano and Stallings, which register is connected to the memory address lines and holds the address of the word being read or written?
questions.explanation: Memory is addressed only through MAR (AR in Mano's basic computer); at the start of fetch the PC value is first copied into MAR. MBR holds the data word and IR the current instruction.

questions.questionText: In Stallings's classification of processor registers, which of the following is a control and status register rather than a user-visible register?
questions.explanation: Stallings lists PC, IR, MAR and MBR as the registers essential to instruction execution, which programs do not name directly. General-purpose, data, index and stack-pointer registers are user-visible because instructions refer to them.

questions.questionText: In a single-accumulator CPU, what does the one-address instruction ADD X (X is a direct memory address) do?
questions.explanation: The accumulator is the implied second operand and the destination, so the word at address X is added to AC and the sum stays in AC. AC ← AC + X would be immediate addressing, and AC ← M[X] is a load.

questions.questionText: An 8-bit ALU adds the 2's-complement numbers 0111 1111 and 0000 0001. Which flag values result? (C = carry out, Z = zero, S = sign, V = overflow)
questions.explanation: 127 + 1 = 128 gives 1000 0000. No carry leaves bit 7 (C = 0), the result is non-zero (Z = 0) with MSB 1 (S = 1), and two positive operands produced a negative result, so V = 1 (carry into the sign bit 1, carry out 0).

questions.questionText: What does the register-transfer statement P: R2 ← R1 mean?
options: The contents of R1 are moved into R2 and R1 is then cleared
When P is 1, the contents of R2 are copied into R1
When the control condition P is 1, the contents of R1 are copied into R2 at the clock edge; R1 is unchanged
The contents of R1 and R2 are exchanged whenever P is 0
questions.explanation: A transfer copies the source into the destination without altering the source, and the control function before the colon enables it only when it equals 1.

questions.questionText: A common bus for 32 registers of 64 bits each is built from multiplexers. What does it need?
options: 64 multiplexers of size 32 × 1, each with 5 select lines
32 multiplexers of size 64 × 1, each with 6 select lines
64 multiplexers of size 32 × 1, each with 32 select lines
5 multiplexers of size 64 × 1, each with 6 select lines
questions.explanation: One multiplexer is needed per bus bit (64), each choosing among the 32 registers (32 × 1), and log2 32 = 5 select lines, shared by all the multiplexers, pick the source register.

questions.questionText: A common bus for 8 registers of 16 bits each is built with three-state buffers instead of multiplexers. How many buffers and what decoder does it need?
questions.explanation: Every bit of every register needs its own buffer: 8 × 16 = 128. Only one register may drive the bus at a time, so a 3 × 8 decoder (log2 8 = 3 inputs) enables one group of 16 buffers.

questions.questionText: Which of the following is a logic micro-operation?
questions.explanation: XOR works bit by bit with no carries, which makes it a logic micro-operation. The other three are an arithmetic, a shift and a memory-transfer micro-operation.

questions.questionText: Register A = 1100 1010 and B = 1111 0000. The selective-complement micro-operation inverts the bits of A in the positions where B has 1s. What is the new value of A?
questions.explanation: Selective complement is A ← A ⊕ B: 1100 1010 ⊕ 1111 0000 = 0011 1010. OR would give 1111 1010 (selective set) and AND would give 1100 0000 (mask).

questions.questionText: Which logic micro-operation clears the bits of A in exactly the positions where B has 1s and leaves the other bits of A unchanged?
questions.explanation: ANDing with the complement of B forces 0 wherever B is 1 and passes A wherever B is 0 (selective clear). A ∧ B is the mask operation, which clears the bits where B has 0s.

questions.questionText: A 4-bit arithmetic circuit computes D = A + Y + Cin, where multiplexers supply Y = B for S1S0 = 00, B' for 01, all 0s for 10 and all 1s for 11. With A = 0110 and B = 0011, what are D and the carry out when S1 S0 Cin = 0 1 1?
questions.explanation: S1S0 = 01 selects Y = B' = 1100 and Cin = 1, so D = 0110 + 1100 + 1 = 1 0011: D = 0011 (6 − 3 = 3) with Cout = 1, meaning no borrow. Without the carry-in (S1 S0 Cin = 010) the result would be 0010.

questions.questionText: In Mano's basic computer the interrupt cycle saves the return address in memory word 0 and clears IEN. Which two instructions, in order, end a typical interrupt service routine?
options: BUN 0 I (indirect branch through word 0), then ION
ION, then BUN 0 I (indirect branch through word 0)
IOF, then BUN 0 (direct branch to word 0)
questions.explanation: The interrupt cycle cleared IEN, so the routine re-enables interrupts with ION and then returns with BUN 0 I, which loads PC with the return address saved in M[0]. ION must come first because nothing placed after the BUN is ever executed. A new interrupt is entered only after BUN 0 I completes, when PC already holds the return address. A direct BUN 0 would jump to word 0 itself, and BSA 0 would overwrite the saved address.

questions.questionText: Stallings writes the fetch cycle as t1: MAR ← (PC); t2: MBR ← Memory, PC ← (PC) + I; t3: IR ← (MBR). Why is IR ← (MBR) placed in t3 rather than in t2?
options: PC must be incremented before IR can be loaded
IR can be loaded only after decoding of the opcode has begun
MBR is being loaded from memory in t2, and a register must not be written and read in the same time unit
Loading IR and reading memory need the same ALU
questions.explanation: Micro-operations grouped in one time unit must not conflict: reading MBR while it is being written would give an unpredictable (old) value. PC ← (PC) + I and MBR ← Memory use different registers, so they can share t2.

questions.questionText: With registers built from edge-triggered flip-flops, what does the statement T: R1 ← R2, R2 ← R1 do when T = 1?
options: R1 and R2 exchange their contents at the same clock edge
Both registers end up with the original contents of R2
Both registers end up with the original contents of R1
Nothing, because an exchange is illegal in RTL and always needs a third register
questions.explanation: Both registers sample their inputs at the same clock edge, when each input still carries the other register's old value, so the contents swap in one clock pulse. Both registers would end up equal only if the two transfers were done one after the other.

questions.questionText: Mano's basic computer has one 16-bit common bus, and its adder and logic circuit takes inputs directly from AC and DR and loads its result into AC. Which pair of micro-operations can be executed in the same clock cycle?
questions.explanation: Only one source can drive the bus in a clock. DR ← AC uses the bus with AC as the source, while AC ← DR goes through the adder and logic circuit without the bus, so both fit in one clock. Each other pair needs two different bus sources (PC and AC, AR and memory, memory and PC).

questions.questionText: An 8-bit register holds 1011 0010. What does it hold after one arithmetic shift right?
questions.explanation: An arithmetic shift right moves every bit one place right and keeps the sign bit, so 1011 0010 (−78) becomes 1101 1001 (−39). A logical shift right would insert 0 and give 0101 1001.

questions.questionText: An arithmetic shift left is applied to an 8-bit 2's-complement register R. For which initial value does the shift overflow?
questions.explanation: Overflow occurs when bits R7 and R6 differ before the shift (Vs = R7 ⊕ R6), because the sign would change. 0100 0000 is +64 and +128 does not fit in 8 bits; the others become −128, +126 and −62, which are all in range.

questions.questionText: Each stage of an arithmetic circuit adds a bit of A, a multiplexer output Y and a carry; Y is B, B', all 0s or all 1s for S1S0 = 00, 01, 10 and 11 respectively, and Cin is the carry into the first stage. What operation results from S1 = 1, S0 = 1 and Cin = 0?
questions.explanation: S1S0 = 11 makes Y all 1s, which is −1 in 2's complement, and with Cin = 0 the circuit computes D = A + 11…1 = A − 1. With Cin = 1 the same selection gives A − 1 + 1 = A (transfer).

questions.questionText: In Mano's basic computer, which kind of instruction is indicated after decoding when D7 = 1 and I = 0?
options: The start of the interrupt cycle
questions.explanation: Opcode 111 (D7 = 1) is not a memory-reference instruction; the mode bit then distinguishes register-reference (I = 0) from input-output (I = 1) instructions.

questions.questionText: In a register-reference instruction of Mano's basic computer (hex 7xxx), how is the particular operation (CLA, CMA, INC, HLT and so on) identified?
options: The opcode field IR(12–14) is decoded a second time
Each of bits IR(0)–IR(11) stands for one operation, and the bit that is 1 selects it
The 12-bit field IR(0–11) is a binary code for up to 4096 operations
The I bit and the address field together form a 13-bit operation code
questions.explanation: The low 12 bits are not an address here: one bit position is set per instruction (for example CLA = 7800 uses bit 11 and HLT = 7001 uses bit 0), and the control unit uses the signals B0–B11 taken from those bits.

questions.questionText: In Mano's basic computer, what does the instruction word B1A4 (hex) specify?
options: STA with indirect addressing; address field 1A4
LDA with direct addressing; address field 1A4
STA with direct addressing; address field B1A
BUN with indirect addressing; address field 1A4
questions.explanation: B = 1011: bit 15 is I = 1 (indirect) and bits 14–12 = 011 are the STA opcode; bits 11–0 give the address 1A4. A direct STA would be 31A4, and an indirect BUN would be C1A4.

questions.questionText: In Mano's basic computer the instruction BSA 135 (direct) is stored at address 020 (all values hex). What do M[135] and PC contain after it executes?
questions.explanation: PC has already been incremented to 021 during fetch. BSA executes D5T4: M[AR] ← PC, AR ← AR + 1 and D5T5: PC ← AR, so the return address 021 is stored at 135 and execution continues at 136, the first instruction of the subroutine.

questions.questionText: In Mano's basic computer (16-bit words), the instruction ISZ X at address 050 (hex) is executed when M[X] = FFFF (hex). What are M[X] and PC afterwards?
questions.explanation: ISZ reads the word, increments it (FFFF + 1 wraps to 0000 in 16 bits), writes it back and, because the result is zero, increments PC once more. PC was 051 after fetch, so the next instruction is skipped and PC = 052.

questions.questionText: In Mano's basic computer PC = 020, AC = 0010, M[020] = 9123, M[123] = 0456 and M[456] = 00F0 (all hex). What does AC hold (hex) after the instruction at 020 is executed?
questions.explanation: 9123 = 1001 0001 0010 0011: I = 1, opcode 001 (ADD), address 123. Indirect addressing takes the effective address from M[123] = 0456, and the operand M[456] = 00F0 is added: AC = 0010 + 00F0 = 0100.

questions.questionText: Mano's basic computer has a 20 ns clock and runs LDA 100 (direct), ADD 101 (indirect), STA 102 (direct) and HLT. With Mano's timing (fetch and decode in T0–T2, T3 always used for the indirect check by memory-reference instructions, register-reference instructions executed in T3), how long does it take from the first T0 until HLT has executed?
questions.explanation: LDA ends at T5 (6 cycles), ADD at T5 (6; the indirect read uses the T3 that every memory-reference instruction spends anyway), STA at T4 (5) and HLT at T3 (4): 21 cycles × 20 ns = 420 ns.

questions.questionText: In Mano's basic computer an interrupt is recognised when PC = 255 (hex). Where is the return address, and what is PC, at the end of the interrupt cycle?
questions.explanation: The interrupt cycle is RT0: AR ← 0, TR ← PC; RT1: M[AR] ← TR, PC ← 0; RT2: PC ← PC + 1, IEN ← 0, R ← 0, SC ← 0. The return address 255 is saved in word 0 and the next fetch is from word 1, which holds a branch to the service routine.

questions.questionText: In Mano's basic computer, under what condition is the interrupt flip-flop R set to 1?
options: IEN = 0 and FGI = 1, at any timing signal
FGI or FGO is 1 at T0, whatever the value of IEN
IEN = 1 and both FGI and FGO are 1, only at T2
IEN = 1 and FGI or FGO is 1, while the timing signal is not T0, T1 or T2
questions.explanation: The control function is T0'T1'T2'(IEN)(FGI + FGO): R ← 1. Excluding T0–T2 keeps the fetch and decode steps intact; the interrupt cycle then starts in place of the next fetch.

questions.questionText: During the interrupt cycle of Mano's basic computer, which register briefly holds the return address before it is written into memory?
questions.explanation: At RT0 the computer executes AR ← 0 and TR ← PC in the same clock, and at RT1 the value in TR is written to M[0]. AR cannot hold it because it must carry the address 0.

questions.questionText: Why does the last micro-operation of every instruction in Mano's basic computer include SC ← 0?
options: To clear the accumulator before the next instruction
So that the next timing signal is T0 and the fetch of the next instruction begins
To disable interrupts until the next instruction is fetched
To reset the program counter to address 0
questions.explanation: The sequence counter SC drives the 4 × 16 timing decoder; clearing it makes T0 active in the next clock, which restarts the fetch sequence with AR ← PC.

questions.questionText: In Mano's basic computer, AR is loaded from the bus by the micro-operations AR ← PC, AR ← IR(0–11) and AR ← M[AR]. Which Boolean function drives the LD (load) input of AR?
questions.explanation: AR ← PC occurs at R'T0, AR ← IR(0–11) at R'T2 and the indirect read AR ← M[AR] at D7'IT3, and ORing these control functions gives the gate. AR ← 0 at RT0 uses CLR(AR), and AR ← AR + 1 at D5T4 uses INR(AR).

questions.questionText: A hardwired control unit needs 12 distinct timing signals T0–T11. How many flip-flops are needed if they are generated by a Johnson (twisted-ring) counter with decoding gates?
questions.explanation: A Johnson counter with n flip-flops passes through 2n states, so 12 states need 12 / 2 = 6 flip-flops, each state decoded by a 2-input AND gate. A ring counter would need 12 flip-flops, and a binary counter with a 4 × 16 decoder needs 4.

questions.questionText: In Mano's basic computer the longest instruction, ISZ, finishes at T6. If the sequence counter and its decoder had to provide only the timing signals that are actually used, what is the minimum width of SC?
questions.explanation: T0 to T6 are 7 distinct states, and ceil(log2 7) = 3 bits (with a 3 × 8 decoder) covers them. Mano uses a 4-bit SC and a 4 × 16 decoder, which leaves spare timing signals.

questions.questionText: Adding a new machine instruction to a CPU with a hardwired control unit normally requires:
options: Only writing a new routine into the control memory
Redesigning the control logic (gates, decoders and their wiring)
Only adding an entry to the opcode mapping ROM
Only enlarging the general-purpose register file
questions.explanation: In a hardwired unit every control signal is a fixed Boolean function of the decoded opcode, timing signals and flags, so a new instruction changes those functions and therefore the circuit. Rewriting control memory is how a microprogrammed unit is changed.

questions.questionText: In Stallings's model of the control unit, which of the following is NOT an input to the control unit?
options: The opcode in the instruction register
The memory address held in MAR
questions.explanation: The control unit's inputs are the clock, the instruction register, the flags and control signals from the control bus (such as interrupt requests). MAR receives control signals; its address is not information the control unit uses.

questions.questionText: According to Stallings, which of the following is NOT one of the things the CPU must do when executing instructions?
options: Interpret the instruction to determine the action required
Fetch data from memory or an I/O module when the instruction needs it
Write the result to memory or I/O when the instruction requires it
Translate high-level-language statements into machine instructions
questions.explanation: Stallings's list is fetch instruction, interpret instruction, fetch data, process data and write data. Translation into machine code is done by a compiler before execution, not by the CPU.

questions.questionText: Why can a stack-organised computer use zero-address arithmetic instructions such as ADD?
options: The operands are always held in AC and DR
The operand values are embedded in the instruction as immediate data
The operands are implicitly the top two stack items, and the result replaces them on the top
The ALU reads its operands directly from I/O ports
questions.explanation: ADD pops the two top items, adds them and pushes the sum, so no address field is needed; SP implies where the operands are.

questions.questionText: In a memory stack that grows toward lower addresses and whose SP points to the current top item, how is a PUSH performed?
questions.explanation: SP must first move to the free word below the current top, and the new item is then written there. Writing before decrementing would overwrite the current top, incrementing suits a stack that grows upward, and the last option is a POP.

questions.questionText: A memory stack grows toward lower addresses and SP = 2000 when it is empty. PUSH is SP ← SP − 1, M[SP] ← DR, and POP is DR ← M[SP], SP ← SP + 1. After PUSH X, PUSH Y, PUSH Z and one POP, which item is on top and what is SP?
options: Y is on top and SP = 1998
Y is on top and SP = 2002
Z is on top and SP = 1997
X is on top and SP = 1999
questions.explanation: The pushes store X at 1999, Y at 1998 and Z at 1997, leaving SP = 1997. The POP reads Z and returns SP to 1998, so Y at address 1998 is now the top.

questions.questionText: Mano's 64-word register stack starts empty with SP = 0. PUSH is SP ← SP + 1, M[SP] ← DR, and POP is DR ← M[SP], SP ← SP − 1. After PUSH A, PUSH B, PUSH C, PUSH D, POP, POP and PUSH E, what is SP and in which word is E stored?
options: SP = 5 and E is in word 5
SP = 3 and E is in word 4
SP = 2 and E is in word 2
SP = 3 and E is in word 3
questions.explanation: The four pushes fill words 1–4 (SP = 4). The two pops read D and then C, leaving SP = 2. PUSH E increments SP to 3 and writes E into word 3, the word that held C.

questions.questionText: What is the reverse Polish (postfix) form of A × (B + C) − D / E?
questions.explanation: B + C becomes B C +, multiplying by A gives A B C + ×, D / E becomes D E /, and the final subtraction comes last. The other strings evaluate (A + B) × C − D / E, A × (B + C − D / E) and (A + B × C − D) / E.

questions.questionText: A stack computer evaluates the postfix expression 8 2 3 × + 6 2 / −. What is the result, and what is the largest number of items on the stack at any moment?
questions.explanation: Trace: 8; 8 2; 8 2 3 (depth 3); × leaves 8 6; + leaves 14; 14 6; 14 6 2 (depth 3); / leaves 14 3; − leaves 14 − 3 = 11. The item popped first is the right operand; reversing it for the final − gives −11.

questions.questionText: In which CPU bus organisation can R3 ← R1 + R2 be completed in a single clock period without temporary registers at the ALU?
options: Single-bus organisation with Y and Z registers
Three-bus organisation (two source buses and one destination bus)
questions.explanation: With two source buses both operands reach the ALU at once, and the third bus carries the result straight into R3, so the transfer and the addition take one clock. A single bus can carry only one word per clock.

questions.questionText: In a single-bus CPU (Hamacher's organisation), why are the temporary registers Y and Z placed at the ALU?
options: Y and Z hold the opcode and address fields during decoding
They buffer memory data to match the slower memory speed
The bus carries only one word per clock, so one operand waits in Y and the result waits in Z until the bus is free
They save the return address during interrupts
questions.explanation: The ALU needs two inputs and produces an output, but a single bus holds only one value at a time. R3 ← R1 + R2 therefore takes three steps: R1 → Y; R2 + Y → Z; Z → R3.

questions.questionText: A register-to-register ADD needs 3 execution steps on a single-bus CPU and 1 step on a three-bus CPU, and instruction fetch takes 3 steps on both. The single-bus CPU is clocked at 1 GHz and the three-bus CPU at 800 MHz, one step per clock. How long does each take to execute 1000 such instructions?
questions.explanation: Single-bus: (3 + 3) steps × 1 ns × 1000 = 6 µs. Three-bus: (3 + 1) steps × 1.25 ns (1 / 800 MHz) × 1000 = 5 µs. Leaving out the fetch steps, or using 0.8 ns as the period, gives the other figures.

questions.questionText: An 8-bit ALU computes A − B as A + B' + 1 with A = 0011 1100 and B = 0110 0100 (2's complement). What is the result, and what are the raw adder carry-out C, the sign S and the overflow V?
questions.explanation: B' + 1 = 1001 1100, and 0011 1100 + 1001 1100 = 1101 1000 with no carry out of bit 7 (C = 0, a borrow because A < B unsigned). The result is 60 − 100 = −40 (S = 1), which fits in 8 bits, so V = 0.

questions.questionText: Register A = 0110 1010. To insert the pattern 1001 into its upper four bits, A is first ANDed with 0000 1111 and then ORed with 1001 0000. What is the final value of A?
questions.explanation: The mask step clears the upper half: 0110 1010 ∧ 0000 1111 = 0000 1010. ORing with 1001 0000 then sets the new bits, giving 1001 1010. Skipping the mask would give 1111 1010.

subtopics.title: Microprogrammed Control: Control Memory & Microinstructions
subtopics.subtitle: Control words in ROM, the sequencer, address sequencing and Mano's 20-bit microinstruction

concepts.text: Control Memory and Control Words

In a microprogrammed control unit the control signals for each step of an instruction are not produced by wired logic but are stored as binary words. The set of control signals active in one clock period is a control word; a control word stored in memory is a microinstruction; a sequence of microinstructions that carries out one machine instruction is a microprogram (a routine); and the memory that holds all the routines is the control memory. Because the microprograms rarely change, control memory is usually a ROM; a writable control memory allows dynamic microprogramming, where microcode is loaded from disk at start-up.
The pieces of a microprogrammed control unit (Mano's organisation):
items: Control address register (CAR): holds the address of the microinstruction currently being read from control memory.
Control memory (ROM): holds the microprogram; each word is one microinstruction.
Control data register (pipeline register): holds the microinstruction just read, so that its control bits can drive the datapath while the next address is being formed.
Next-address generator (microprogram sequencer): computes the next value of CAR from the current microinstruction, external status bits and the instruction opcode.
Subroutine register (SBR): saves the return address when a microprogram subroutine is called.

concepts.text: Address Sequencing

Each machine instruction has its own routine in control memory, and all instructions share a fetch routine and an effective-address routine. Executing an instruction therefore means: run the fetch routine, run the address routine, then jump to the routine for this opcode, and at its end return to fetch. The sequencer must provide the address transitions that make this possible.
Four ways in which the next microinstruction address can be formed:
items: Incrementing CAR: the normal case, CAR ← CAR + 1, moving to the next word of the current routine.
Branching, unconditional or conditional: the address field of the microinstruction is loaded into CAR, either always or only when a selected status bit (indirect bit, sign, zero) is 1.
Mapping: after fetch, the opcode bits of the instruction are transformed into the starting address of that instruction's routine, either by a fixed bit pattern or through a small mapping ROM.

Subroutine call and return: CAR + 1 is saved in SBR and CAR is loaded with the subroutine address; at the end CAR ← SBR restores the return address. The effective-address computation is the usual shared subroutine.

concepts.text: Mano's Microinstruction Format

Mano's example computer has a 128 × 20 control memory. Each microinstruction has three microoperation fields F1, F2 and F3 of 3 bits each, a 2-bit condition field CD, a 2-bit branch field BR and a 7-bit address field AD: 3 + 3 + 3 + 2 + 2 + 7 = 20 bits. Up to three microoperations (one from each field, chosen so they do not conflict) execute in one clock; the CD and BR fields together tell the sequencer how to form the next address. Because the opcode is 4 bits, mapping places routine starting addresses at 0 xxxx 00, giving each instruction 4 consecutive words.

concepts.plainText: Microinstruction length = F1 + F2 + F3 + CD + BR + AD = 3+3+3+2+2+7 = 20 bits

rows: CAR ← AD if condition true, else CAR ← CAR + 1
SBR ← CAR + 1, CAR ← AD if condition true, else CAR + 1

concepts.text: The microoperation codes of the three F fields (000 is NOP in every field):
items: F1: 001 ADD (AC ← AC + DR), 010 CLRAC, 011 INCAC, 100 DRTAC (AC ← DR), 101 DRTAR (AR ← DR(0–10)), 110 PCTAR (AR ← PC), 111 WRITE (M[AR] ← DR).
F2: 001 SUB, 010 OR, 011 AND, 100 READ (DR ← M[AR]), 101 ACTDR (DR ← AC), 110 INCDR, 111 PCTDR (DR(0–10) ← PC).
F3: 001 XOR, 010 COM (AC ← AC'), 011 SHL, 100 SHR, 101 INCPC, 110 ARTPC (PC ← AR), 111 reserved.
A symbolic microinstruction is written as LABEL: MICROOPS CD BR AD, one per line; the assembler converts it to the 20-bit word.

concepts.text:
ORG 64                        ; fetch routine
FETCH: PCTAR      U JMP NEXT       ; AR <- PC
       READ, INCPC U JMP NEXT      ; DR <- M[AR], PC <- PC + 1
       DRTAR      U MAP            ; AR <- DR(0-10), jump to opcode routine
ORG 0                         ; ADD routine
ADD:   NOP        I CALL INDRCT    ; if I = 1 fetch effective address
       READ       U JMP NEXT       ; DR <- M[AR]
       ADD        U JMP FETCH      ; AC <- AC + DR, back to fetch
INDRCT: READ      U JMP NEXT       ; subroutine: DR <- M[AR]
       DRTAR      U RET            ; AR <- DR(0-10), return
Horizontal vs Vertical, and vs Hardwired

rows: One bit per control signal, little or no encoding
Fields heavily encoded; decoders regenerate signals
Usually one or a few per word

concepts.text: Microprogrammed control compared with hardwired control:
items: Advantages: systematic design, easy to modify or extend the instruction set, supports emulation of another machine, simpler to debug, and fewer random-logic errors in complex CISC control units.
Disadvantages: slower because every micro-step needs a control-memory access, the control memory costs chip area, and the hardware to support it (sequencer, mapping logic) is itself non-trivial.
Hardwired control wins on speed and is used in RISC designs; microprogrammed control historically dominated CISC machines such as the VAX and early x86.

concepts.text: Worked example: a control memory of 128 words of 20 bits. The number of words fixes the address width, 128 = 2^7, so CAR and the AD field are 7 bits. If the design grew to 1024 microinstructions, CAR would need 10 bits and every microinstruction would lengthen by 3 bits in its AD field. The word length, 20 bits here, is fixed by how many control fields are packed into one microinstruction, not by the size of the memory.
Going Deeper: Sizing, Sequencing and Timing Microprograms

A microinstruction is sized field by field. Signals that may be active together each need their own bit, as in a horizontal format. A group of k signals that are never active together, such as the sources that drive one bus, can share an encoded field of ceil(log2(k + 1)) bits, because one code must mean 'none of them'. A condition-select field that chooses among c status bits plus 'always true' needs ceil(log2(c + 1)) bits, the branch-type field needs enough bits to name each kind of address transition, and the next-address field needs log2 N bits for an N-word control memory.

concepts.plainText: w = h direct bits + sum over encoded groups of ceil(log2(ki + 1)) + ceil(log2(c + 1)) condition bits + b branch-type bits + log2 N address bits

concepts.text:
Worked example 1: sizing a microinstruction
Given: 2K-word control memory, 12 independent signals,
       groups of 6, 15 and 3 mutually exclusive micro-operations,
       10 status conditions plus 'always', 4 branch types
Direct field         : 12 bits
Group of 6  (+ none) : ceil(log2 7)  = 3 bits
Group of 15 (+ none) : ceil(log2 16) = 4 bits
Group of 3  (+ none) : ceil(log2 4)  = 2 bits
Condition select     : ceil(log2 11) = 4 bits
Branch type          : log2 4        = 2 bits
Next address         : log2 2048     = 11 bits
Word = 12 + 3 + 4 + 2 + 4 + 2 + 11 = 38 bits
Control memory = 2048 x 38 = 77,824 bits = 9.5 KiB
One bit per signal in the groups would give 12 + 24 + 4 + 2 + 11 = 53 bits

rows: How the next address is obtained
The tested condition picks one of two explicit addresses in the word
CAR + 1 normally; the AD field on a true branch; SBR on RET; the mapped opcode on MAP
One address field; needs an incrementer and a multiplexer
Control words fall through to CAR + 1; separate branch words carry the condition and address
Shortest word; each branch costs an extra microinstruction
Opcode mapping (fixed bits or mapping ROM)
The opcode forms the routine's start address after fetch
Fixed bits waste unused words; a ROM allows any placement

concepts.text: Mano's sequencer is a 4 × 1 multiplexer in front of CAR whose inputs are CAR + 1, the AD field, SBR and the mapped opcode address. A second 4 × 1 multiplexer, steered by CD, picks the status bit T (U, I, S or Z), and small input logic turns BR and T into the select lines. JMP and CALL take AD when T = 1 and CAR + 1 when T = 0, CALL also loads SBR with CAR + 1 but only when the branch is taken, and RET and MAP ignore T altogether. A CALL whose condition is false therefore behaves exactly like a step to the next word.

Worked example 2: EXCHANGE with I = 1 (opcode 0011 maps to 0 0011 00 = 12)
CAR  Microinstruction          Effect                 Next CAR
64   PCTAR U JMP NEXT          AR <- PC               65
65   READ, INCPC U JMP NEXT    DR <- M[AR], PC+1      66
66   DRTAR U MAP               AR <- DR(0-10)         12
12   NOP I CALL INDRCT         I = 1: SBR <- 13       67
67   READ U JMP NEXT           DR <- M[AR]            68
68   DRTAR U RET               AR <- DR(0-10)         13 (from SBR)
13   READ U JMP NEXT           DR <- M[AR]            14
14   ACTDR, DRTAC U JMP NEXT   AC and DR swap         15
15   WRITE U JMP FETCH         M[AR] <- DR            64
Total: 9 microinstructions (7 when I = 0)

Long microprograms often repeat the same control word many times. A two-level store keeps each distinct word once in a nanomemory and replaces every microinstruction with a short pointer to it. For example, 1024 microinstructions of 120 bits containing only 128 distinct words need 1024 × 120 = 122,880 bits in one level, but only 1024 × 7 + 128 × 120 = 7,168 + 15,360 = 22,528 bits in two levels, about 18% of the original. The price is a second memory access in every step, and the Motorola 68000 is a well-known processor that used such a microcode and nanocode pair.

concepts.latex: S_{2} = N \lceil \log_{2} U \rceil + U\,w \quad \text{versus} \quad S_{1} = N\,w
concepts.plainText: Two-level store S2 = N × ceil(log2 U) + U × w bits, versus one level S1 = N × w (N microinstructions, U distinct words of w bits)

concepts.text: Timing rules for microprogrammed control:
items: Instruction time = (fetch-routine words + effective-address words when used + execute words) × microinstruction cycle; weight any optional part by how often it runs.

Without a pipeline register the microinstruction cycle is control-memory access time plus datapath time; with one it is the larger of the two, because the next word is read while the current one executes.
A branch that tests a status bit produced by the current microinstruction cannot be overlapped in the same way and can cost an extra cycle.
A hardwired unit produces each step's signals within a few gate delays, so the same sequence of steps runs faster; microprogramming trades that speed for ease of change.

concepts.text: Common slips: forgetting the 'none' code when encoding a group (8 signals need 4 bits, not 3); sizing the address field from the word length instead of the number of words; counting the fetch routine only once for a whole program; treating micro-operations in different fields of one word as sequential (they all take effect at the same clock edge); and assuming that CALL loads SBR even when its condition is false.

For a sizing question, write one line per field with its bit count before adding them, and check every encoded field for a 'none' code and the condition field for an 'always' code. For a Mano trace, list the CAR values in order: fetch 64, 65, 66, then the mapped address 4 × opcode, with 67 and 68 inserted whenever I = 1 leads to the INDRCT subroutine.

formulas.plainText: CAR bits = log2(number of microinstructions); 128 words need 7 bits
Microinstruction length = sum of field widths = 20 bits in Mano's format
Control memory size = 2^n words × w bits per word (128 × 20 = 2560 bits)
Mapping: CAR = 0, four opcode bits, 00, giving 4 words per routine

notes.text: Learn the CD and BR tables as pairs: CD 00 U, 01 I, 10 S, 11 Z; BR 00 JMP, 01 CALL, 10 RET, 11 MAP. A frequent MCQ gives a 20-bit word and asks which field is which, or gives 128 × 20 and asks for the CAR width (7).
The number of words in control memory sets the address width; the word length sets how many control fields fit. 128 × 20 means 7-bit addresses and 20-bit words, not the other way round.

Only one microoperation per F field can be chosen per word, and the three chosen must not conflict (e.g. F1 = ADD and F2 = SUB both write AC). That is why the routine for one instruction usually needs several microinstructions.
A microprogram subroutine differs from a machine-language subroutine: the return address is kept in SBR, a single register, so nesting of microprogram calls is normally one level deep.

formulas.title: CAR width
formulas.plainText: n = log2(number of microinstructions)
formulas.description: The control address register and the AD field need n bits for a control memory of 2^n words; 128 words need 7 bits.

formulas.title: Microinstruction length
formulas.latex: w = F_1 + F_2 + F_3 + CD + BR + AD
formulas.description: Mano's microinstruction is 20 bits: three 3-bit microoperation fields, 2-bit condition, 2-bit branch, 7-bit address.

formulas.title: Control memory size
formulas.plainText: bits = 2^n words × w bits/word
formulas.description: Total ROM capacity of the control memory; 128 × 20 = 2560 bits.

flashcards.front: Define control word, microinstruction, microprogram and control memory.
flashcards.back: A control word is the set of control signals for one clock; stored in memory it is a microinstruction; a sequence of them for one machine instruction is a microprogram; the ROM holding all microprograms is the control memory.

flashcards.front: Name the four ways the next microinstruction address is formed.
flashcards.back: Increment CAR; unconditional or conditional branch to the AD field; mapping from the instruction opcode to a routine start address; subroutine call (save CAR + 1 in SBR) and return (CAR ← SBR).

flashcards.front: What do the CD codes 00, 01, 10, 11 and BR codes 00, 01, 10, 11 mean in Mano's microinstruction?
flashcards.back: CD: U (always), I (indirect bit), S (sign of AC), Z (AC zero). BR: JMP, CALL, RET, MAP.

flashcards.front: Horizontal vs vertical microinstruction in one line each.
flashcards.back: Horizontal: one bit per control signal, long words, many parallel microoperations, fast. Vertical: encoded fields, short words, needs decoders, slower but compact.

questions.questionText: A microprogrammed control unit has a control memory of 128 words, each 20 bits long. The control address register (CAR) must be:
questions.explanation: 128 = 2^7, so 7 address bits select any of the 128 microinstructions. The 20-bit word length does not affect the address width.

questions.questionText: Which of the following is NOT one of the four status conditions selected by the CD field of Mano's 20-bit microinstruction?
questions.explanation: The CD field selects U (always 1), I (DR(15)), S (AC(15)) or Z (AC = 0). The E flip-flop belongs to the basic computer's hardwired design, not to the microprogrammed example.

questions.questionText: A control unit must generate 48 control signals, any combination of which may be active in the same clock. How wide is the control field of a purely horizontal microinstruction?
questions.explanation: A horizontal format gives every control signal its own bit, so any combination can be specified: 48 bits. Six bits (ceil(log2 48)) could name only one signal at a time.

questions.questionText: Who proposed microprogramming in 1951 as a systematic way to design the control unit of a computer?
questions.explanation: Maurice Wilkes of Cambridge suggested storing the control signals of each step as words in a control memory, which is the basis of microprogrammed control.

questions.questionText: A control unit has 30 control signals split into four groups of 8, 16, 4 and 2 signals. Within a group at most one signal is active at a time, and each group must also be able to encode 'no signal active'. What is the minimum width of the encoded control field?
questions.explanation: Each group needs ceil(log2(k + 1)) bits: ceil(log2 9) = 4, ceil(log2 17) = 5, ceil(log2 5) = 3 and ceil(log2 3) = 2, a total of 14 bits. Forgetting the 'none' code gives 3 + 4 + 2 + 1 = 10.

questions.questionText: Which register in a microprogrammed control unit plays the same role for microinstructions that the program counter plays for machine instructions?
questions.explanation: CAR holds the control-memory address of the microinstruction to be read next, and the sequencer increments or loads it, just as PC is incremented or loaded for the main program.

questions.questionText: The condition-select field of a microinstruction must choose one of 8 status bits or an 'always true' condition for unconditional branches. How many bits does the field need?
questions.explanation: There are 8 + 1 = 9 choices and ceil(log2 9) = 4 bits. Three bits cover only 8 choices, which leaves no code for 'always'.

questions.questionText: In Mano's microprogrammed computer the microinstruction at control address 65 is READ, INCPC U JMP NEXT (READ is F2 code 100 and INCPC is F3 code 101). What is its 20-bit binary form, written as F1 F2 F3 CD BR AD?
questions.explanation: F1 is NOP (000), F2 = READ (100), F3 = INCPC (101), CD = U (00) and BR = JMP (00); NEXT means address 65 + 1 = 66 = 1000010. Using 65 itself, or the MAP code 11, are the typical slips.

questions.questionText: Mano's control memory holds the word 000 000 000 01 01 1000011 (F1 F2 F3 CD BR AD) at address 0. What does this microinstruction do?
options: NOP I CALL 67: if the indirect bit is 1, save 1 in SBR and go to 67
NOP U JMP 67: always go to 67
NOP I JMP 67: if the indirect bit is 1, go to 67 without saving a return address
NOP S CALL 67: if AC is negative, save 1 in SBR and go to 67
questions.explanation: All three F fields are 000 (no micro-operation); CD = 01 selects I, BR = 01 is CALL and AD = 1000011 = 67, the INDRCT subroutine. When I = 1 the sequencer stores CAR + 1 = 1 in SBR and loads 67 into CAR.

questions.questionText: Microprograms stored in a control memory are commonly referred to as:
questions.explanation: Microcode sits between hardware and software: it is stored permanently, usually in ROM, and is called firmware.

questions.questionText: Mano's fetch routine ends with DRTAR U MAP at address 66. DR holds the instruction 1 0010 00000101011 (I bit, 4-bit opcode, 11-bit address). Which address is loaded into CAR?
questions.explanation: MAP loads CAR(2–5) from the opcode DR(11–14) = 0010 and clears the other bits, so CAR = 0 0010 00 = 8, the start of the STORE routine. Using the opcode alone gives 2, and including the I bit gives 1001000 = 72.

questions.questionText: A control unit with a 10-bit CAR maps each 5-bit opcode to the routine address 1 x x x x x 0 0 0 0 (a 1, the opcode, then four 0s). How many consecutive words can each routine occupy before reaching the next opcode's routine, and at which decimal address does the routine for opcode 00011 start?
questions.explanation: Four trailing zeros leave 2^4 = 16 words per opcode. Opcode 00011 gives 10 0011 0000 in binary = 512 + 48 = 560; dropping the leading 1 would give 48.

questions.questionText: Opcodes are 6 bits long, and the control memory holds 1024 microinstructions. What size must a mapping ROM be if it gives the starting address of each opcode's routine?
questions.explanation: The ROM is addressed by the opcode (2^6 = 64 words), and each word must hold a full control-memory address of log2 1024 = 10 bits. A mapping ROM lets routines start anywhere instead of at a fixed bit pattern.

questions.questionText: In Mano's microprogrammed control unit, where is the return address saved when a microprogram subroutine is called?
options: On a stack in main memory
questions.explanation: CALL stores CAR + 1 in SBR and loads the subroutine address into CAR, and RET copies SBR back into CAR. Main-memory location 0 is used by the basic computer's interrupt cycle, not by microprogram calls.

questions.questionText: In Mano's microprogrammed computer an ADD instruction with I = 1 (indirect) is executed. In what order are control-memory addresses visited, from the start of the fetch routine until CAR returns to FETCH?
questions.explanation: Fetch runs 64–66 and MAP sends opcode 0000 to address 0, where NOP I CALL INDRCT saves 1 in SBR and jumps to 67. INDRCT (67, 68) reads the effective address and RET returns to 1; words 1 and 2 read the operand and add it, and word 2 jumps back to FETCH.

questions.questionText: In Mano's microprogrammed computer a BRANCH instruction is executed while AC(15) = 0 (AC not negative). How many microinstructions are executed, counting the fetch routine, before control returns to FETCH?
questions.explanation: Fetch uses 64, 65 and 66, and MAP goes to 4. There NOP S JMP OVER finds S = 0 and falls through to 5, where NOP U JMP FETCH returns: 64, 65, 66, 4, 5 = 5 microinstructions.

questions.questionText: What is the purpose of the control data register (pipeline register) at the output of the control memory?
options: It stores the return address of a microprogram subroutine
It converts the instruction opcode into a routine starting address
It buffers data words passing between main memory and the CPU
It holds the current microinstruction so that its control bits drive the datapath while the next address is formed and read
questions.explanation: Latching the microinstruction frees the control memory for the next access while the present word executes. SBR stores return addresses, the mapping logic converts opcodes and MBR buffers memory data.

questions.questionText: Mano's microprogrammed computer executes ADD (I = 0), STORE (I = 1), BRANCH (I = 0, with AC(15) = 1) and EXCHANGE (I = 0), in that order. Each microinstruction takes 100 ns. Counting every fetch routine, how long do the four instructions take?
questions.explanation: ADD: 64, 65, 66, 0, 1, 2 = 6; STORE with the INDRCT call: 64–66, 8, 67, 68, 9, 10 = 8; BRANCH taken: 64–66, 4, 6, 7 = 6; EXCHANGE: 64–66, 12–15 = 7. The total is 27 × 100 ns = 2.7 µs.

questions.questionText: A control memory that can be written, so that the microprogram can be loaded from disk at start-up or changed later, makes possible:
questions.explanation: With a writable control store the microcode is not fixed in ROM, so it can be replaced while the system is in service, for example to fix errors or to add instructions.

questions.questionText: In Mano's BRANCH routine the word at address 6 (OVER) is NOP I CALL INDRCT. When a BRANCH with AC(15) = 1 and I = 1 reaches it, what value is stored in SBR?
questions.explanation: CALL saves CAR + 1 = 6 + 1 = 7 in SBR before loading 67, the address of INDRCT. After INDRCT's RET the routine continues at 7 with ARTPC U JMP FETCH.

questions.questionText: A microprogram has 2048 microinstructions of 200 bits each, but only 256 of them are different. It is rebuilt as a two-level store: a micromemory of pointers into a nanomemory that holds the 256 distinct 200-bit words. What is the total storage of the two-level scheme?
questions.explanation: Each pointer needs log2 256 = 8 bits: micromemory 2048 × 8 = 16,384 bits plus nanomemory 256 × 200 = 51,200 bits gives 67,584 bits. A single-level store would need 2048 × 200 = 409,600 bits.

questions.questionText: Which statement about horizontal microinstructions is NOT correct?
options: Many micro-operations can be activated in the same clock
The word is long because each control signal has its own bit
Each field has to be decoded before its control signals can be applied
Little or no decoding logic is needed, so they are fast
questions.explanation: Needing a decoder for every field describes vertical (encoded) microinstructions. A horizontal word uses one bit per signal, which makes it long, highly parallel and fast.

questions.questionText: Reading a microinstruction from control memory takes 40 ns, and carrying out its micro-operations in the datapath takes 30 ns. With a pipeline register the next microinstruction is read while the current one executes. Ignoring branch effects, what is the microinstruction cycle time?
questions.explanation: With overlap the cycle is set by the slower of the two stages: max(40, 30) = 40 ns. Without the pipeline register the steps are in series: 40 + 30 = 70 ns.

questions.questionText: A control memory has 512 words. Each microinstruction has 20 directly controlled signals (one bit each), two encoded fields for groups of 7 and 12 mutually exclusive micro-operations (each field must also encode 'none'), a condition-select field for 8 status bits or 'always true', a 2-bit branch-type field and a next-address field. How long is the microinstruction?
questions.explanation: Direct 20 + ceil(log2 8) = 3 + ceil(log2 13) = 4 + condition ceil(log2 9) = 4 + branch 2 + address log2 512 = 9 gives 42 bits. Forgetting 'always' gives 41, leaving out the address gives 33, and one bit per signal in the groups gives 54.

questions.questionText: When is a two-level (nanoprogrammed) control store most attractive?
options: When many microinstructions in a long microprogram are identical, so each can be replaced by a short pointer into a small nanomemory
When the microprogram is short and every microinstruction is different
When the control unit must be as fast as possible
When the instruction set is small and regular, as in RISC processors
questions.explanation: Nanoprogramming stores each distinct wide word once and replaces the copies with pointers, which saves space at the cost of a second memory access in every step.

questions.questionText: A 1K-word control memory holds microinstructions with three encoded fields for groups of 4, 8 and 3 mutually exclusive micro-operations (each field also encodes 'none'), 5 directly controlled bits, a 2-bit branch-type field, a 2-bit condition-select field and a next-address field. What is the total size of the control memory?
questions.explanation: The encoded fields need ceil(log2 5) = 3, ceil(log2 9) = 4 and ceil(log2 4) = 2 bits; adding 5 + 2 + 2 and log2 1024 = 10 address bits gives 28 bits, and 1024 × 28 = 28,672 bits. Without the 'none' codes the word is 26 bits (26,624), and without the address field 18 bits (18,432).

questions.questionText: Which capability follows naturally from microprogrammed control and is hard to obtain with hardwired control?
options: Executing each instruction in fewer clock cycles than a hardwired unit
Emulating the instruction set of another computer by loading a different microprogram
Removing the need for an instruction register
questions.explanation: Because the instruction set is defined by the microcode, a different microprogram lets the same hardware run another machine's instructions; several IBM System/360 models used this to run programs written for older IBM computers.

questions.questionText: Which of the following is NOT a way in which a microprogram sequencer forms the next microinstruction address?
options: Loading the address field when a selected condition is true
Copying the program counter (PC) into CAR
Mapping the opcode bits to a routine starting address
questions.explanation: The sequencer increments CAR, branches to the address field (conditionally or not), maps the opcode, or calls and returns through SBR. PC addresses machine instructions in main memory, not microinstructions.

questions.questionText: In a microprogrammed CPU every instruction runs a 3-microinstruction fetch routine and an execute routine averaging 4 microinstructions, and 40% of instructions also call a 2-microinstruction effective-address subroutine. Each microinstruction takes 60 ns. What is the average instruction time?
questions.explanation: Average microinstructions per instruction = 3 + 4 + 0.4 × 2 = 7.8, and 7.8 × 60 ns = 468 ns. Counting the subroutine for every instruction gives 540 ns, ignoring it gives 420 ns and leaving out the fetch routine gives 288 ns.

questions.questionText: In the variable-format microinstruction technique, one bit says whether a word is a control microinstruction or a branch microinstruction. What is the main drawback?
options: Every microinstruction must carry two full address fields
A branch needs a microinstruction of its own, because the bits that normally carry control signals hold the branch condition and address instead
The control memory must be writable
CAR can no longer be incremented between microinstructions
questions.explanation: Sharing the bits keeps the words short, but a branch word issues no control signals, so routines take extra cycles. Two explicit address fields in every word are the drawback of a different technique.

questions.questionText: A datapath has 64 control signals. A horizontal format uses a 64-bit control field. A vertical format activates exactly one signal per microinstruction, using a code that must also allow 'no operation'. For a routine of 10 steps, each activating 3 signals at once, how many control-field bits does each format use (address fields ignored)?
questions.explanation: Horizontal: 10 words × 64 bits = 640. Vertical: 65 codes need ceil(log2 65) = 7 bits and each step needs 3 words, so 30 × 7 = 210 bits; 6-bit codes would give 180, and one word per step 70.

questions.questionText: Which of the following is NOT an advantage of microprogrammed control over hardwired control?
options: Easier modification or extension of the instruction set
A systematic design that simplifies complex control units
Higher operating speed with the same technology
Design errors can be corrected by changing the microcode
questions.explanation: Microprogrammed control is slower, because every step needs a control-memory read. Its benefits are flexibility, a systematic design and easy correction.

questions.questionText: A vertical microinstruction has a single micro-operation field that encodes 100 distinct micro-operations plus a no-operation code. How many bits does this field need?
questions.explanation: 101 codes are needed, and 2^6 = 64 < 101 ≤ 128 = 2^7, so 7 bits are required. One bit per micro-operation (100 bits) would be the horizontal choice.

questions.questionText: Why do most RISC processors use hardwired control?
options: They have too many instructions to fit into a control memory
Their simple, fixed-format instructions complete in about one clock, and reading a control memory for each step would lengthen that clock
Hardwired control is easier to modify when instructions are added
Microprogrammed control cannot be combined with any form of pipelining
questions.explanation: RISC designs aim at about one instruction per cycle with a short cycle time, and hardwired decoding avoids the control-memory access delay. Large, irregular instruction sets are where microprogramming pays off.

questions.questionText: A microinstruction has 40 control bits, a 6-bit condition-select field and two explicit next-address fields (one used when the condition is true, the other when it is false) for a 4K-word control memory. How long is the microinstruction?
questions.explanation: Each address field needs log2 4096 = 12 bits, so the word is 40 + 6 + 2 × 12 = 70 bits. With a single address field it would be 58 bits.

questions.questionText: Mano's EXCHANGE routine contains the microinstruction ACTDR, DRTAC U JMP NEXT. Why does it swap AC and DR correctly?
options: F1 executes before F2, so DR is copied into AC first and AC into DR afterwards
The sequencer inserts a hidden temporary register between F1 and F2
Only DRTAC executes; ACTDR is ignored because both use the bus
Both transfers are triggered by the same clock edge, so each register receives the other's old contents
questions.explanation: DRTAC (F1 = 100) and ACTDR (F2 = 101) are in different fields and take effect together at the end of the clock period, when both registers still hold their old values. If they ran one after the other, both registers would end up with the same value.

questions.questionText: Which pair of micro-operations cannot be specified together in one of Mano's 20-bit microinstructions because they are coded in the same field?
questions.explanation: READ (100) and ACTDR (101) are both F2 codes, and a field holds only one code. INCPC is in F3 while PCTAR and DRTAR are in F1, so the other pairs are legal; READ, INCPC is in fact the second word of the fetch routine.

questions.questionText: A control memory of 16 KiB (1 KiB = 1024 bytes) holds 64-bit microinstructions. How many microinstructions does it hold, and how wide must CAR be?
questions.explanation: 16 KiB = 16 × 1024 × 8 = 131,072 bits, and 131,072 / 64 = 2048 words, so CAR needs log2 2048 = 11 bits. Dividing the byte count by 64 without converting to bits gives 256.

questions.questionText: Mano's mapping 0 xxxx 00 gives each opcode four consecutive control words. What is done if a new instruction's routine needs six microinstructions?
options: The routine starts at its mapped address and continues, through a jump, in free words elsewhere in control memory
The instruction cannot be implemented in this control unit
The mapping hardware automatically allocates eight words to that opcode
The extra microinstructions are placed in main memory
questions.explanation: The first words sit at the mapped address, and a JMP in the last of them transfers to spare control words (for example above the fetch and INDRCT words), where the routine is completed and returns to FETCH.

questions.questionText: An ADD instruction with I = 0 reaches control address 0, where Mano's microinstruction is NOP I CALL INDRCT. What does the sequencer do?
questions.explanation: With the condition false, CALL behaves like a branch not taken: CAR is simply incremented and the SBR load signal stays inactive. Only when I = 1 does it store 1 in SBR and jump to 67.

questions.questionText: What does the mapping process in a microprogrammed control unit do?
options: Converts a virtual address into a physical main-memory address
Converts the opcode of a machine instruction into the starting address of its routine in control memory
Assigns each micro-operation to a field of the microinstruction
Copies the control memory into a cache at start-up
questions.explanation: After fetch, the opcode bits are transformed, by a fixed bit arrangement or a mapping ROM, into a control-memory address, so the sequencer can jump to that instruction's microroutine.

questions.questionText: In Mano's 128-word control memory the fetch routine is placed at address 64. Why?
options: Address 64 is the reset address of every control ROM
Addresses 0–63 are reserved for the interrupt cycle
A routine that starts at a power of two runs faster
The mapping 0 xxxx 00 puts every opcode routine in addresses 0–63, so 64–127 are free for fetch and shared subroutines
questions.explanation: With a 0 in the top bit of the mapped address, all 16 opcodes × 4 words fall in the lower half of control memory. The upper half, starting at 64, holds FETCH and INDRCT.

questions.questionText: In a microprogrammed CPU, how is one machine-language instruction carried out?
options: By a routine of one or more microinstructions read from control memory
By one machine-language subroutine stored in main memory
By a single state of a hardwired sequence counter
questions.explanation: Each machine instruction is interpreted by its own microroutine: after the shared fetch routine, the mapped routine issues the control words that perform the instruction.

questions.questionText: In Mano's microinstruction format, what is the AD field used for when BR = 10 (RET)?
options: It is added to SBR to form the return address
It is not used, because CAR is loaded from SBR
questions.explanation: RET selects the SBR input of the sequencer multiplexer whatever the condition, so the address field is ignored; in the binary microprogram the AD field of such a word is simply 0000000.

questions.questionText: Which statement about Mano's microprogrammed control unit is NOT correct?
options: With BR = CALL and a false condition, CAR is simply incremented
With BR = MAP, the next address comes from the opcode whatever the CD field selects
Enlarging the control memory from 128 to 256 words requires wider F1, F2 and F3 fields
The U condition is always 1, so U JMP is an unconditional branch
questions.explanation: More control words need one more address bit, in CAR and the AD field (7 to 8 bits); the F fields depend only on the micro-operations they encode. The other three statements describe the sequencer correctly.

questions.questionText: Which fields of Mano's 20-bit microinstruction go to the next-address logic (sequencer) rather than being decoded into datapath micro-operations?
questions.explanation: CD selects the status bit to test, BR chooses the kind of address transition and AD supplies the branch address, while the F fields are decoded into register-transfer signals.

questions.questionText: A control memory holds 2K microinstructions of 48 bits each. What is its capacity in KiB (1 KiB = 1024 bytes)?
questions.explanation: 2048 × 48 = 98,304 bits = 12,288 bytes = 12 KiB. Dividing the bit count by 1024 without first converting to bytes gives 96.

questions.questionText: An instruction set of 40 instructions needs execute routines averaging 6 microinstructions each, plus a shared 3-word fetch routine and a 2-word effective-address subroutine. The number of control-memory words must be a power of two. Each microinstruction has 36 control bits, a 3-bit condition field, a 2-bit branch field and a next-address field. What is the minimum control memory size?
questions.explanation: Words needed = 40 × 6 + 3 + 2 = 245, rounded up to 256, so the address field is 8 bits and a word is 36 + 3 + 2 + 8 = 49 bits: 256 × 49 = 12,544 bits. Not rounding up gives 245 × 49 = 12,005, and dropping the address field gives 256 × 41 = 10,496.

subtopics.title: Instruction Formats, Addressing Modes & Data Manipulation
subtopics.subtitle: Three- to zero-address formats, effective-address rules and the instruction classes

concepts.text: Instruction Fields and Address Formats

A machine instruction is a binary word divided into fields. The operation code (opcode) says what to do, a mode field says how to interpret the address part, and one or more operand or address fields say where the data is. Instructions may be fixed length (typical of RISC, one word each) or variable length (typical of CISC). How many address fields an instruction carries depends on the CPU organisation: a general-register machine allows two or three, a single-accumulator machine needs only one because the accumulator is implied, and a stack machine needs none for arithmetic because the operands are the top two stack entries. The standard way to compare formats is to code the same expression, X = (A + B) × (C + D), where A, B, C, D and X are memory locations. Three-address instructions give the shortest program but the longest instruction words; zero-address (stack) instructions are the shortest but need the most of them; one-address (accumulator) code needs a temporary memory location T.

; three-address (general register CPU)
ADD  R1, A, B        ; R1 <- M[A] + M[B]
ADD  R2, C, D        ; R2 <- M[C] + M[D]
MUL  X,  R1, R2      ; M[X] <- R1 * R2
; two-address (one operand is also the destination)
MOV  R1, A           ; R1 <- M[A]
ADD  R1, B           ; R1 <- R1 + M[B]
MOV  R2, C           ; R2 <- M[C]
ADD  R2, D           ; R2 <- R2 + M[D]
MUL  R1, R2          ; R1 <- R1 * R2
MOV  X,  R1          ; M[X] <- R1

; one-address (accumulator CPU)
LOAD  A              ; AC <- M[A]
ADD   B              ; AC <- AC + M[B]
STORE T              ; M[T] <- AC
LOAD  C              ; AC <- M[C]
ADD   D              ; AC <- AC + M[D]
MUL   T              ; AC <- AC * M[T]
STORE X              ; M[X] <- AC

; zero-address (stack CPU); PUSH and POP carry an address
PUSH A               ; TOS <- M[A]
PUSH B               ; TOS <- M[B]
ADD                  ; TOS <- (A + B)
PUSH C               ; TOS <- M[C]
PUSH D               ; TOS <- M[D]
ADD                  ; TOS <- (C + D)
MUL                  ; TOS <- (C + D) * (A + B)
POP  X               ; M[X] <- TOS
Addressing Modes

The addressing mode is the rule that turns the address field of an instruction into the effective address (EA), the actual location of the operand, or into the operand itself. Modes exist to shorten instructions, to support pointers, loops, arrays and relocatable code, and to give the programmer flexibility. Some modes need no memory reference for the operand (implied, immediate, register), some need one (direct, register indirect, relative, indexed, base), and indirect needs two.

rows: Operand fixed by the opcode itself
CMA (complement AC); all zero-address stack instructions
ADD R1, #5; no memory access; good for constants
Operand in the register named by the field
ADD R1, R2; fastest, short field
ADD R2, (R1); register holds a pointer
LDA 500; one memory access for the operand
LDA @500 or LDA (500); two memory accesses
BR +8; PC already advanced; position-independent branches
LDA 200(X); XR steps through an array
Base register holds start of segment; field is displacement; supports relocation
EA = register, then register ← register + 1 (or + word size)
LDA −(R1); walks a table backward; stack push

concepts.latex: EA_{rel} = PC + A,\quad EA_{idx} = XR + A,\quad EA_{ind} = M[A]
concepts.plainText: Relative EA = PC + A; indexed EA = XR + A; indirect EA = M[A]

concepts.text: Worked example: an instruction at address 400 with address field 500 has already advanced PC to 401 when the effective address is computed. Direct mode gives EA = 500; immediate mode gives the operand 500 itself; relative mode gives EA = 401 + 500 = 901; if XR = 100, indexed mode gives EA = 600; if M[500] = 800, indirect mode gives EA = 800. Numeric questions of this kind are common, so always ask whether PC has been incremented before the relative addition.
Data Transfer and Data Manipulation Instructions
Data transfer instructions move data without changing it:
items: Load (memory to register) and store (register to memory); move (register to register, or in some machines any to any); exchange (swap two registers or a register and a memory word).
Push and pop transfer a word between a register or memory and the top of the stack, adjusting the stack pointer.
Input and output move a word between a register and an I/O port; in memory-mapped I/O the ordinary load and store instructions do this.

The same load can appear with several addressing modes (LD ADR direct, LD @ADR indirect, LD R1 register, LD (R1) register indirect, LD #NBR immediate, LD $ADR relative, LD ADR(X) indexed), each a different opcode or mode bit pattern.

concepts.text: Data manipulation instructions compute on data and update the flags:
items: Arithmetic: increment, decrement, add, subtract, multiply, divide, add with carry, subtract with borrow, negate (2's complement); available for signed/unsigned integers and often floating point and BCD.

Logical and bit manipulation: clear, complement, AND (mask bits), OR (set bits), exclusive-OR (toggle bits), plus flag control such as clear carry, set carry, complement carry, enable and disable interrupt.
Shift: logical, arithmetic and circular (rotate) in both directions, one bit or n bits per instruction, with the carry flag optionally included in the rotation.

rows: SHL: 0 into LSB, MSB to carry
SHR: 0 into MSB, LSB to carry
SHLA: like SHL; overflow if sign changes
SHRA: sign bit copied into MSB
Signed multiply/divide by 2 with sign preserved
No bit lost; used in CRC and bit-field work
ROLC: carry into LSB, MSB into carry
RORC: carry into MSB, LSB into carry

concepts.text: Program control instructions change the flow of execution instead of the data: branch and jump (conditional on the status bits C, S, Z, V or unconditional), skip, call and return for subroutines using the stack, and compare and test, which perform a subtraction or an AND only to set the flags. Interrupts are a hardware-initiated form of program control that saves the return address and status, then transfers to a service routine.
Going Deeper: Field Sizing, Expanding Opcodes and Flags

Every field of an instruction must be wide enough for the largest value it has to name. An opcode that distinguishes N operations needs ⌈log2 N⌉ bits, a register field for R registers needs ⌈log2 R⌉ bits, a mode field for M addressing modes needs ⌈log2 M⌉ bits, and a direct address into a word-addressable memory of 2^n words needs n bits. The instruction length is the sum of its fields; when the length is fixed (say one 32-bit word) the fields compete, so whatever is left after the others decides the number of opcodes or the range of an immediate or displacement.
