A k-bit two's-complement field covers −2^(k−1) to 2^(k−1) − 1.

concepts.latex: L = \lceil \log_2 N_{op} \rceil + \lceil \log_2 M \rceil + r\lceil \log_2 R \rceil + a\,n
concepts.plainText: Length = ceil(log2 N_op) + ceil(log2 M) + r × ceil(log2 R) + a × n, for r register fields and a address fields of n bits

concepts.text:
Worked example 1: one-word 32-bit instruction, fields opcode | mode | reg | address
Memory 128K x 32, word-addressable: 128K = 2^17  -> address field 17 bits
40 registers: 2^5 = 32 < 40 <= 64 = 2^6         -> register field  6 bits
5 addressing modes: 4 < 5 <= 8                    -> mode field      3 bits
Opcode = 32 - 17 - 6 - 3                          -> opcode field    6 bits
Operations available = 2^6 = 64
Format: | opcode 6 | mode 3 | reg 6 | address 17 |

Expanding opcodes exploit the fact that an instruction with fewer address fields has spare bits. The designer leaves some patterns of the short opcode unused; each unused pattern, followed by the bits of an address field that the next format no longer needs, opens a whole block of longer opcodes. If a k-bit opcode field has U patterns in use and the next format releases an a-bit address field, 2^k − U patterns remain and each expands into 2^a new opcodes. Giving the commonest instructions the short opcodes also brings the average opcode length down, much like a variable-length code.

concepts.plainText: Opcodes available at the next level = (2^k − U) × 2^a

concepts.text:
Worked example 2: 16-bit instructions with 6-bit address fields
Two-address : opcode = 16 - 2 x 6 = 4 bits -> 16 patterns; 12 used, 4 free
One-address : 4 free x 2^6 = 256 opcodes;  250 used, 6 free
Zero-address: 6 free x 2^6 = 384 opcodes available
Check       : 12 x 2^12 + 250 x 2^6 + 384 x 1
            = 49152 + 16000 + 384 = 65536 = 2^16 bit patterns

Worked example 3: two-word LOAD at 300-301, address field 250 in word 301
PC = 302 after fetch, R1 = 1200, XR = 40, M[250] = 700 (word-addressable)
Direct            EA = 250
Immediate         operand = 250 itself (read with word 301, no extra access)
Indirect          EA = M[250] = 700 (two data accesses)
Relative          EA = PC + 250 = 302 + 250 = 552
Indexed           EA = XR + 250 = 40 + 250 = 290
Register          operand = R1 = 1200 (no EA)
Register indirect EA = R1 = 1200
Autoincrement     EA = 1200, then R1 = 1201
Autodecrement     R1 = 1199 first, then EA = 1199

The ALU sets the status bits after every data manipulation instruction. For an n-bit result, C is the carry out of the most significant position, S is the most significant bit of the result, Z is 1 when every result bit is 0, and V is 1 when a signed result has overflowed, which happens exactly when two operands of the same sign produce a result of the other sign. A compare instruction forms A − B as A + B' + 1, sets the flags and throws the difference away; with this convention C = 1 means no borrow, that is A ≥ B for unsigned numbers. Unsigned branch conditions therefore test C and Z, while signed conditions test S ⊕ V and Z, because S alone gives the wrong answer whenever overflow occurs.

Worked example 4: 8-bit flags
ADD 0111 1010 (+122) + 0100 0110 (+70)
    carry into bit 7 = 1, carry out of bit 7 = 0
    result 1100 0000 -> S = 1, Z = 0, C = 0, V = 1 xor 0 = 1
    (+192 is outside -128..+127, so the signed result is wrong)
CMP A = 0011 0000 (48), B = 0101 0000 (80)
    A + B' + 1 = 0011 0000 + 1010 1111 + 1 = 1110 0000, carry out 0
    C = 0 (A < B unsigned); S = 1, V = 0, S xor V = 1 (A < B signed)

Common slips: adding the relative offset to the address of the branch instead of the updated PC; incrementing an autoincrement register by 1 instead of by the operand size (4 for a 32-bit word in byte-addressable memory); counting an immediate operand as a memory access; sizing an opcode with ⌊log2 N⌋ instead of ⌈log2 N⌉; multiplying by the opcode width instead of the released address-field width in expanding-opcode problems; and testing S alone for a signed less-than. The C-flag test in the table assumes C = 1 means no borrow; some processors, such as x86, store the borrow instead.

formulas.plainText: Direct EA = A; indirect EA = M[A] (two memory accesses in total)
Relative EA = PC + A, with PC already pointing to the next instruction

formulas.latex: EA_{indexed} = XR + A,\quad EA_{base} = BR + A
formulas.plainText: Indexed EA = XR + A; base-register EA = BR + A
Arithmetic shift right = floor(x/2); arithmetic shift left = 2x (sign preserved)

notes.text: Effective-address MCQs give an instruction address, an address field and PC, XR or memory contents. Remember: relative uses the incremented PC; indirect reads memory once to get EA and again to get the operand; immediate has no EA at all.
Two-address and three-address formats count address fields, not operands. ADD R1, R2 is two-address even though it uses two operands and a result, because the result overwrites R1.
The one-address program above needs a temporary location T because a single accumulator cannot hold both partial sums; the stack machine avoids T because the stack keeps the intermediate value.

formulas.title: Relative addressing
formulas.plainText: EA = PC + A
formulas.description: The address field is added to the (already incremented) program counter; used for short, position-independent branches.

formulas.title: Indexed and base addressing
formulas.latex: EA = XR + A \quad\text{or}\quad EA = BR + A
formulas.plainText: EA = XR + A (indexed) or EA = BR + A (base register)
formulas.description: The address field is added to an index register (array stepping) or a base register (segment relocation).

formulas.title: Indirect addressing
formulas.plainText: EA = M[A], operand = M[M[A]]
formulas.description: The address field points to a memory word that holds the effective address, so the operand costs two memory reads.

formulas.title: Arithmetic shift
formulas.plainText: Arithmetic shift right = floor(x/2); left = 2x
formulas.description: Arithmetic shifts keep the sign bit so they multiply and divide signed numbers by two.

flashcards.front: Write X = (A + B) × (C + D) in zero-address (stack) instructions.
flashcards.back: PUSH A; PUSH B; ADD; PUSH C; PUSH D; ADD; MUL; POP X. Only PUSH and POP carry an address; arithmetic works on the top two stack entries.

flashcards.front: How many memory accesses does each of direct, indirect and immediate addressing need to obtain the operand?
flashcards.back: Direct: one; indirect: two (first the effective address, then the operand); immediate: none, the operand is in the instruction.

flashcards.front: Distinguish logical, arithmetic and circular shifts.
flashcards.back: Logical shifts insert 0 and drop the outgoing bit into the carry; arithmetic shifts keep the sign bit (divide or multiply signed numbers by 2); circular shifts wrap the outgoing bit around to the other end.

flashcards.front: Name the three classes of computer instructions.
flashcards.back: Data transfer (load, store, move, exchange, push, pop, input, output), data manipulation (arithmetic, logical and bit, shift) and program control (branch, jump, call, return, compare, test).

questions.questionText: A processor must support 100 distinct operations. What is the minimum width of its opcode field?
questions.explanation: The opcode needs ⌈log2 100⌉ bits: 2^6 = 64 is too few and 2^7 = 128 ≥ 100, so 7 bits are required.

questions.questionText: A register-to-register instruction names one of 120 operations and three operands chosen from a file of 32 registers. What is the minimum instruction length?
questions.explanation: Opcode = ⌈log2 120⌉ = 7 bits and each register field = log2 32 = 5 bits, so the length is 7 + 3 × 5 = 22 bits.

questions.questionText: A word-addressable memory holds 1M words of 32 bits (1M = 2^20). Each instruction occupies one word and has four fields: an opcode, a mode field selecting one of 5 addressing modes, a register field naming one of 30 registers, and a direct memory address. How wide is the opcode field, and how many opcodes can it encode?
questions.explanation: Address = 20 bits, mode = ⌈log2 5⌉ = 3 bits, register = ⌈log2 30⌉ = 5 bits. Opcode = 32 − 20 − 3 − 5 = 4 bits, which encodes 2^4 = 16 operations.

questions.questionText: A 16-bit fixed-length register-immediate instruction has a 5-bit opcode, one register field for a file of 8 registers, and a two's-complement immediate that uses all the remaining bits. What range of constants can the immediate hold?
questions.explanation: Register field = log2 8 = 3 bits, so the immediate has 16 − 5 − 3 = 8 bits. An 8-bit two's-complement field covers −2^7 to 2^7 − 1, i.e. −128 to +127.

questions.questionText: A computer has 20-bit instructions and 7-bit memory address fields. Two-address instructions use all the remaining bits as their opcode, and 50 two-address instructions are defined. Using expanding opcodes, what is the maximum number of one-address instructions?
questions.explanation: Two-address opcode = 20 − 2 × 7 = 6 bits = 64 patterns, of which 64 − 50 = 14 are free. Each free pattern is extended by the released 7-bit address field: 14 × 2^7 = 1792 one-address instructions.

questions.questionText: A computer has 16-bit instructions and 4-bit address fields; three-address instructions have a 4-bit opcode. With expanding opcodes it defines 14 three-address, 30 two-address and 20 one-address instructions. What is the maximum number of zero-address instructions?
questions.explanation: Three-address: 16 − 14 = 2 free patterns give 2 × 2^4 = 32 two-address codes; 32 − 30 = 2 free give 32 one-address codes; 32 − 20 = 12 free give 12 × 2^4 = 192 zero-address instructions.

questions.questionText: What is the main idea of an expanding-opcode scheme?
options: Instructions that need fewer address bits use the freed bits to extend the opcode, so more operations fit in a fixed instruction length
Every instruction has the same opcode width, and extra operations are supplied by a second instruction word
The opcode is expanded at run time by the microprogram into several microinstructions
The opcode grows with the size of main memory so that more addresses can be reached
questions.explanation: An instruction with fewer address fields has spare bits; unused short-opcode patterns act as escapes that are extended by those bits, giving many more opcodes without lengthening the instruction.

questions.questionText: In a single-accumulator CPU, how many explicit address fields does an ADD instruction need?
options: None; both operands are on a stack
Two; one for each source operand
Three; two sources and a result
One; the accumulator is an implied source and destination
questions.explanation: An accumulator machine executes ADD X as AC ← AC + M[X]: the accumulator is implied, so only the memory address X is written in the instruction.

questions.questionText: Which CPU organisation allows arithmetic instructions with no address field at all?
questions.explanation: In a stack machine ADD, MUL and similar instructions take their operands from the top of the stack and push the result, so they are zero-address; only PUSH and POP carry an address.

questions.questionText: Which statement about three-address instructions is correct?
options: They give the shortest programs for arithmetic expressions but need long instruction words to hold three addresses
They give the longest programs because each instruction does less work
They need no temporary registers or locations for any expression
They are the format used by stack machines for PUSH and POP
questions.explanation: Naming two sources and a destination lets each instruction finish a whole operation, so programs are short, but three address fields make the binary instruction long.

questions.questionText: An accumulator machine provides LOAD M, STORE M, ADD M, SUB M and MUL M, each with one memory address; AC is the implied operand and destination. What is the minimum number of instructions that computes X = (A − B) × (C + D), with all five variables in memory?
questions.explanation: One partial result must be parked in memory because AC cannot hold both A − B and C + D: LOAD A, SUB B, STORE T, LOAD C, ADD D, MUL T, STORE X is 7 instructions.

questions.questionText: X = (A + B) × (C + D) is coded four ways, with A, B, C, D and X in memory: three-address using R1 and R2 (3 instructions), two-address using R1 and R2 (6), one-address using a temporary T (7), and zero-address with the stack held in CPU registers (8). Counting only operand accesses to memory, not instruction fetches, which program makes the most?
options: None; all four programs make exactly 5 accesses
questions.explanation: The three-, two- and zero-address programs each read A, B, C, D once and write X once (5 accesses). The one-address program also stores and reloads T, so each of its 7 instructions touches memory once: 7 accesses.

questions.questionText: A stack machine has 8-bit opcodes and 16-bit memory addresses; PUSH and POP carry one address while ADD and MUL carry none. What is the size of the program PUSH A; PUSH B; ADD; PUSH C; PUSH D; ADD; MUL; POP X?
questions.explanation: The four PUSH and one POP are 8 + 16 = 24 bits each and the three arithmetic instructions are 8 bits each: 5 × 24 + 3 × 8 = 120 + 24 = 144 bits = 18 bytes.

questions.questionText: Which postfix (reverse Polish) sequence does a stack computer evaluate for X = (A + B) × (C − D) / E, with × and / of equal precedence applied left to right?
questions.explanation: A + B and C − D become A B + and C D −; their product is A B + C D − ×, and dividing it by E appends E /. The other strings compute different expressions, e.g. (A + B) × (C − D / E).

questions.questionText: X = A + B × (C − D × E) is converted to postfix by the standard algorithm, keeping the operands in their original order, and run on a zero-address machine (one PUSH per operand, one instruction per operator, then POP X). How many instructions does the program have, and what is the largest number of entries on the stack at any moment?
questions.explanation: The postfix form is A B C D E × − × +: 5 PUSH + 4 operators + POP X = 10 instructions. All five operands are pushed before the first operator (D × E) can run, so the stack reaches 5 entries.

questions.questionText:
On a stack machine, SUB and MUL pop the top two entries and push (second entry op top entry). With A = 10, B = 4 and C = 3 in memory, what value does this program store in X?
PUSH A
PUSH B
SUB
PUSH C
MUL
POP X
questions.explanation: The stack holds 10, 4; SUB leaves 10 − 4 = 6; PUSH C gives 6, 3; MUL leaves 18; POP X stores 18, i.e. X = (A − B) × C.

questions.questionText:
In a two-address machine the first operand is both a source and the destination (ADD R1, B means R1 ← R1 + M[B], and MOV copies the second operand into the first). With A = 2, B = 3 and C = 4, what does this program leave in X?
MOV R1, A
ADD R1, B
MOV R2, R1
MUL R1, C
SUB R1, R2
MOV X, R1
questions.explanation: R1 = 2, then 2 + 3 = 5; R2 = 5; R1 = 5 × 4 = 20; R1 = 20 − 5 = 15; X ← 15. The program computes (A + B) × C − (A + B).

questions.questionText: A two-word instruction occupies addresses 600 and 601 of a word-addressable memory, and its second word holds the address field 350. The PC is incremented after each word is fetched. What is the effective address in relative mode?
questions.explanation: After both words are fetched PC = 602, so EA = PC + address field = 602 + 350 = 952.

questions.questionText: The address field of a LOAD instruction is 300, and memory holds M[300] = 450 and M[450] = 900. What value is loaded into the accumulator if the instruction uses indirect addressing?
questions.explanation: Indirect: EA = M[300] = 450 and the operand is M[450] = 900. Direct mode would load 450 and immediate mode would load 300.

questions.questionText: A two-word LOAD AC instruction is stored at 250–251 (word-addressable) with address field 500 in word 251; after the fetch PC = 252. R1 = 400 and the index register XR = 100. Memory holds M[400] = 700, M[500] = 800, M[600] = 900, M[752] = 650 and M[800] = 300. Which addressing mode loads the value 900 into AC?
questions.explanation: Indexed: EA = XR + 500 = 600, operand M[600] = 900. Relative gives EA = 752 (650), indirect gives EA = M[500] = 800 (300), register indirect gives EA = 400 (700), and direct would load M[500] = 800.

questions.questionText: Memory is byte-addressable and operands are 4-byte words. R3 = 1000 before LOAD R1, (R3)+ (autoincrement) is executed twice in succession. What effective address does the second execution use, and what does R3 hold afterwards?
questions.explanation: Autoincrement uses the register as the EA and then adds the operand size, 4. First execution: EA = 1000, R3 → 1004; second: EA = 1004, R3 → 1008.

questions.questionText: A stack grows toward lower addresses in a byte-addressable memory with 4-byte words, and SP points to the top item. PUSH is MOV −(SP), Rx (autodecrement) and POP is MOV Rx, (SP)+ (autoincrement). Starting with SP = 5000, the program performs three pushes and then one pop. What is SP at the end?
questions.explanation: Each push subtracts 4 before writing and each pop adds 4 after reading: SP = 5000 − 3 × 4 + 4 = 4992.

questions.questionText: A program assembled as if it started at address 0 is loaded at address 24000, and its base register is set to 24000. An instruction in base-register mode has displacement 1350. What is its effective address?
questions.explanation: EA = base register + displacement = 24000 + 1350 = 25350. Only the base register changes when the program is relocated.

questions.questionText: A loop body contains LOAD R1, 2000(XR) (indexed mode) in a byte-addressable memory. XR starts at 0 and is increased by 4 at the end of every iteration. What effective address does the instruction use in the 6th iteration?
questions.explanation: Before the 6th iteration XR has been increased 5 times, so XR = 5 × 4 = 20 and EA = 2000 + 20 = 2020.

questions.questionText: An x86-style memory operand uses EA = base + index × scale + displacement. With base register = 1000, index register = 6, scale = 4 and displacement = 20, what is the effective address?
questions.explanation: EA = 1000 + 6 × 4 + 20 = 1000 + 24 + 20 = 1044. Only the index is scaled; the displacement is added unscaled.

questions.questionText: A 3-byte PC-relative branch instruction starts at address 750 in a byte-addressable memory and must jump to address 700. The offset is added to the PC after the whole instruction has been fetched. What signed offset must the assembler place in the instruction?
questions.explanation: When the offset is added, PC = 750 + 3 = 753, so offset = target − PC = 700 − 753 = −53.

questions.questionText: In a byte-addressable RISC with 32-bit instructions, a branch computes target = (PC + 4) + 4 × offset, where PC is the address of the branch and offset is a signed count of words. A branch at address 40000 has offset −3. What is its target address?
A one-word instruction LOAD @A uses indirect addressing. Counting the instruction fetch, how many memory accesses does it make in total?
questions.explanation: One access fetches the instruction, one reads M[A] to obtain the effective address, and one reads the operand at that address: 3 accesses.

questions.questionText: Once the instruction has been fetched, which addressing mode needs no further memory access to obtain its operand?
questions.explanation: In register mode the operand is already in a CPU register. Direct, register indirect and indexed modes all form an effective address in memory and must read it.

questions.questionText: Which addressing mode lets a branch work unchanged wherever the program is loaded in memory (position-independent code)?
questions.explanation: A PC-relative branch stores the distance from the current PC, which stays the same when the whole program moves; absolute addresses would all need patching.

questions.questionText: Which statement about immediate addressing is NOT correct?
options: The operand is part of the instruction itself
No memory access beyond the instruction fetch is needed for the operand
The largest constant is limited by the width of the operand field
The effective address is the value in the address field
questions.explanation: EA = address field describes direct addressing. In immediate mode the field is the operand itself, so no extra access is needed, but the constant's range is limited by the field width.

questions.questionText: Which of the following is a program control instruction?
questions.explanation: Program control instructions change the PC or test conditions for doing so: branch, jump, call, return, compare and test. XCHG and PUSH are data transfer, and ROL is a data manipulation (shift) instruction.

questions.questionText: How does CMP R1, R2 differ from SUB R1, R2?
options: CMP subtracts R1 from R2 instead of R2 from R1
CMP changes R1 but does not affect the flags
CMP performs R1 − R2 only to set the status flags and discards the difference, leaving R1 unchanged
CMP performs a logical AND instead of a subtraction
questions.explanation: Compare subtracts so that C, S, Z and V are ready for a following conditional branch, but it stores no result; TEST does the same with a logical AND.

questions.questionText: An 8-bit register holds 1100 1010. What does it hold after an exclusive-OR with the mask 1111 0000?
questions.explanation: XOR with 1 complements a bit and XOR with 0 leaves it unchanged, so the high nibble 1100 becomes 0011 and the low nibble 1010 is kept: 0011 1010.

questions.questionText: Which single operation sets bits 7 and 0 of an 8-bit register to 1 while leaving bits 6 to 1 unchanged?
questions.explanation: OR with 1 forces a bit to 1 and OR with 0 keeps it. AND with 1000 0001 would clear bits 6 to 1, and XOR would clear bits 7 and 0 if they were already 1.

questions.questionText: An 8-bit register holds the signed value 1011 0100 (−76). What does it hold after one arithmetic shift right?
questions.explanation: SHRA moves every bit one place right and copies the sign bit into the MSB: 1101 1010 = −38 = −76 / 2. A logical shift right would insert 0 and give 0101 1010.

questions.questionText: An 8-bit register holds 0110 0101 (+101). After one arithmetic shift left, what are the register contents and the overflow condition?
options: 1100 1010; overflow, because the sign bit changed
0100 1010; no overflow, because the sign bit is kept
questions.explanation: SHLA shifts left and inserts 0 at the LSB: 1100 1010. The sign bit changed from 0 to 1 because 2 × 101 = 202 exceeds +127, so overflow is set.

questions.questionText: The carry flag is C = 1 and an 8-bit register holds R = 0100 0001. What are R and C after one rotate right through carry (RORC)?
questions.explanation: RORC shifts right, moves the old carry (1) into the MSB and the old LSB (1) into C, giving R = 1010 0000 and C = 1.

questions.questionText: An 8-bit ALU adds 0110 0100 and 0011 0010. C is the carry out of bit 7, Z is set for a zero result, S is bit 7 of the result and V flags signed overflow. Which flag values result?
questions.explanation: 0110 0100 + 0011 0010 = 1001 0110 (100 + 50 = 150). No carry leaves bit 7 (C = 0), bit 7 is 1 (S = 1), two positive operands gave a negative result (V = 1), and the result is non-zero (Z = 0).

questions.questionText: With the same flag definitions (C = carry out of bit 7, Z = zero, V = signed overflow), an 8-bit ALU adds 1111 0000 and 0001 0000. Which flags are set, and is the 8-bit result correct as an unsigned sum and as a signed sum?
options: C = 1, Z = 1, V = 1: wrong both as unsigned and as signed
C = 0, Z = 1, V = 0: correct both as unsigned and as signed
C = 1, Z = 1, V = 0: wrong as unsigned (240 + 16 = 256 does not fit), correct as signed (−16 + 16 = 0)
C = 1, Z = 0, V = 0: correct as unsigned, wrong as signed
questions.explanation: 1111 0000 + 0001 0000 = 1 0000 0000, so the register holds 0000 0000 with C = 1 and Z = 1. Unsigned 240 + 16 = 256 overflows 8 bits (C = 1), but signed −16 + 16 = 0 is exact, so V = 0.

questions.questionText: After CMP A, B on signed two's-complement numbers, which flag condition means A < B?
questions.explanation: A − B is negative when A < B, but overflow inverts the sign bit, so the reliable test is S ⊕ V = 1. C = 0 is the unsigned 'lower' test when C = 1 means no borrow.

questions.questionText: A CPU performs CMP A, B by forming A + B' + 1 in 8 bits, with A = 0110 0100 (+100) and B = 1100 1110 (−50). Which flags result, and is 'branch if less than (signed)', which tests S ⊕ V = 1, taken?
options: S = 1, V = 0; the branch is taken
S = 1, V = 1; the branch is taken
S = 0, V = 0; the branch is not taken
S = 1, V = 1; the branch is not taken
questions.explanation: A + B' + 1 = 0110 0100 + 0011 0001 + 1 = 1001 0110, so S = 1; two positive addends gave a negative result, so V = 1 (+150 does not fit). S ⊕ V = 0, so A ≥ B and the branch is not taken, which is right because +100 > −50.

questions.questionText: Two unsigned 8-bit numbers, 200 and 100, are added. Which status flag shows that the true sum does not fit in 8 bits?
questions.explanation: 300 exceeds 255, so a carry leaves bit 7 and C = 1 while the register keeps 300 − 256 = 44. V reports signed overflow, a different condition (here −56 + 100 = 44, so V = 0).

questions.questionText: A CPU keeps a memory stack that grows toward lower addresses, with SP pointing to the top item. Which microoperation sequence correctly implements CALL to a subroutine at effective address EA?
options: PC ← EA; SP ← SP − 1; M[SP] ← PC
M[SP] ← PC; SP ← SP + 1; PC ← EA
SP ← SP − 1; M[SP] ← PC; PC ← EA
questions.explanation: The return address (the PC, already pointing at the next instruction) must be pushed before PC is overwritten, and a push onto a downward-growing stack decrements SP first. PC ← M[SP]; SP ← SP + 1 is the RETURN sequence.

questions.questionText: Which of the following is a difference between a program interrupt and a subroutine call?
options: An interrupt is started by a hardware or internal signal rather than by an instruction, and the CPU saves its status (PSW) as well as the return address
An interrupt always returns to the instruction that caused it, while a call returns to the next instruction
A subroutine call saves every CPU register automatically, while an interrupt saves nothing
An interrupt transfers control to the address in the current instruction's address field
questions.explanation: A subroutine call is an instruction whose address field gives the target and which saves only the PC. An interrupt is triggered by a signal, its service-routine address comes from hardware, and the CPU state (PSW) is saved too.

questions.questionText: An accumulator machine has 3-byte instructions (1-byte opcode, 2-byte address) and 4-byte data words. It runs LOAD A; ADD B; STORE T; LOAD C; ADD D; MUL T; STORE X. Counting both instruction fetches and data transfers, how many bytes move between the CPU and memory?
questions.explanation: Code: 7 instructions × 3 bytes = 21 bytes fetched. Data: each instruction reads or writes one 4-byte word, 7 × 4 = 28 bytes. Total = 21 + 28 = 49 bytes.

subtopics.title: RISC vs CISC
subtopics.subtitle: Two design philosophies, register windows, the CPI argument and modern convergence

concepts.text: CISC: Complex Instruction Set Computers

Early computers had tiny memories and were programmed in assembly, so designers kept adding powerful instructions that did more work per word of program: one instruction might load two operands from memory, multiply them and store the result. The result is a complex instruction set with hundreds of opcodes, many instruction lengths and many addressing modes. Such instructions need several clock cycles and are most easily implemented with a microprogrammed control unit. The Intel x86 family, the DEC VAX and IBM System/370 are the classic examples.
Characteristics of CISC:
items: Large instruction set (often 200 or more) with variable-length instruction words (x86: 1 to 15 bytes).
Many addressing modes (5 to 20) and instructions that operate directly memory-to-memory, so a single instruction may access memory several times.
Instructions take a variable number of cycles; average CPI is high (typically 2 to 6 without micro-op tricks).
Microprogrammed control unit, which makes complex instructions manageable but adds control-memory delay.
Relatively few general-purpose registers, because register space was spent on decode logic and microcode; compilers historically produced short programs.

concepts.text: RISC: Reduced Instruction Set Computers

Studies in the late 1970s (IBM 801, Berkeley RISC, Stanford MIPS) showed that compilers used only a small fraction of a CISC instruction set, and that simple instructions dominated execution. RISC removes the rarely used instructions and modes, makes every instruction one word long and one cycle long, and lets only load and store touch memory. The freed chip area goes into registers and a hardwired control unit, and the uniform instruction shape makes pipelining straightforward. ARM, MIPS, SPARC, PowerPC and RISC-V are RISC designs.
Characteristics of RISC:
items: Few instructions (typically under 100 to 150) with a fixed-length format (32 bits), so decoding is simple and fast.
Few addressing modes (usually register, immediate and register plus displacement).
Load/store architecture: arithmetic works only on registers; only LOAD and STORE reference memory.
Hardwired control unit and one instruction completed per clock cycle (CPI close to 1) using an instruction pipeline.
Large register file (32 or more) and often overlapped register windows; heavy reliance on an optimising compiler.

concepts.text: Side by Side

Overlapped register windows (Berkeley RISC) attack the cost of procedure calls. The register file is divided into windows, one per active procedure; each procedure sees a fixed set of global registers plus its own window, and adjacent windows overlap so that parameters passed to a callee sit in the registers shared between the two windows without any memory traffic. A call simply moves the window pointer, and a return moves it back. With G global registers, L local registers per window, C common (overlapped) registers between neighbours and W windows, a procedure sees G + L + 2C registers and the file holds (L + C)W + G registers in total. Berkeley RISC I used G = 10, L = 10, C = 6, W = 8: 32 registers visible, 138 in total.

concepts.latex: N_{reg} = (L + C)W + G,\quad \text{window size} = L + 2C + G
concepts.plainText: Total registers = (L + C)W + G; registers visible per procedure = L + 2C + G

concepts.text: Examples and the Performance Argument

x86 (Intel and AMD) is the surviving CISC line: variable-length instructions, rich modes, a long history of backward compatibility. ARM (phones, embedded, Apple M-series), MIPS (routers, older consoles), SPARC and the open RISC-V standard are RISC lines. Embedded designs favour RISC because fixed-length, single-cycle instructions give predictable timing and low power; desktop and server software stayed on x86 largely because of the installed base of binaries.

concepts.plainText: CPU time = instruction count × cycles per instruction × clock period

concepts.text: The performance argument is the classic CPU time equation. CISC lowers the instruction count IC but raises CPI; RISC raises IC (more, simpler instructions) but brings CPI to about 1 and permits a shorter clock period because each stage does less. Experience showed that the RISC side wins: a 30 to 50 percent increase in instruction count is more than paid for by a two- to three-fold reduction in CPI and a faster clock. Compare two implementations by computing IC × CPI × T for each rather than by counting instructions alone.

Modern processors have converged. Since the Pentium Pro, x86 chips decode each CISC instruction into one or more fixed-length micro-operations (micro-ops) that a RISC-like pipelined, superscalar core executes; frequently used simple instructions are hardwired and only rare complex ones fall back to microcode. Meanwhile RISC families have added multiply-accumulate, SIMD and compressed 16-bit instruction encodings (ARM Thumb, RISC-V C). The instruction-set argument today is mostly about code density, decoder power and licensing rather than raw speed.
Going Deeper: CPI, MIPS and Register Windows

The CPU time equation comes from counting clock cycles: a program needs a certain number of cycles, each lasting T = 1/f, and the number of cycles equals the instructions executed (IC) times the average cycles per instruction (CPI). When instructions fall into classes with different cycle counts, CPI is the average of the class CPIs weighted by the fraction of executed (dynamic) instructions in each class, not by how often they appear in the listing. Roughly, IC depends on the instruction set and the compiler, CPI on the organisation and the instruction set, and the clock period on circuit technology and organisation. RISC and CISC push these factors in opposite directions, so only their product decides which is faster.

concepts.plainText: CPI = Σ f_i × CPI_i (f_i = fraction of instructions in class i); CPU time = IC × CPI / f

concepts.text:
Worked example 1: weighted CPI, time and MIPS
Mix: ALU 50% (1 cycle), load 20% (2), store 10% (2), branch 20% (3)
CPI  = 0.5x1 + 0.2x2 + 0.1x2 + 0.2x3 = 0.5 + 0.4 + 0.2 + 0.6 = 1.7
IC   = 2 x 10^6 instructions, f = 400 MHz (T = 2.5 ns)
Time = 2 x 10^6 x 1.7 x 2.5 ns = 8.5 ms
MIPS = f / (CPI x 10^6) = 400 / 1.7 = 235.3

MIPS (million instructions per second) equals IC / (T_CPU × 10^6), or f / (CPI × 10^6), and MFLOPS counts only floating-point operations: FP operations / (T_CPU × 10^6). Both are rates of doing something, not measures of getting the job done. A RISC machine executes more, simpler instructions for the same work, so its MIPS figure flatters it; on one machine a code sequence with many cheap instructions can raise MIPS while taking longer; and MFLOPS treats a divide like an add. Execution time for the same program is the only fair comparison.

Worked example 2: a higher MIPS rating but a slower program
Classes A, B, C take 1, 2 and 4 cycles; clock 500 MHz
Code 1: 4M A + 2M B + 1M C -> cycles = 4 + 4 + 4 = 12M, IC = 7M
        time = 12M / 500 MHz = 24 ms, MIPS = 7 / 0.024 = 291.7
Code 2: 8M A + 1M B + 1M C -> cycles = 8 + 2 + 4 = 14M, IC = 10M
        time = 14M / 500 MHz = 28 ms, MIPS = 10 / 0.028 = 357.1
Code 2 has the higher MIPS rating yet takes 28 / 24 = 1.17 times as long.

In the circular-buffer organisation of overlapped windows, a current-window pointer (CWP) selects the running procedure's window; a call advances CWP by one window, so the caller's outgoing registers become the callee's incoming registers, and a return moves CWP back. Because the windows form a ring, the outgoing registers of the newest window would overlap the incoming registers of the oldest one, so an N-window file holds at most N − 1 procedure activations. A call that would go deeper raises a window-overflow trap that saves the oldest window's incoming and local registers to memory, and a return into a saved procedure raises a window-underflow trap that reloads them. Call depth in real programs usually moves within a narrow band, so these traps are rare.

Worked example 3: a SPARC-style file with 8 windows
Each window: 8 in, 8 local, 8 out; 8 global registers
Map to the formula: G = 8, L = 8, C = 8 (outs of one window = ins of the next)
Visible per procedure = G + L + 2C = 8 + 8 + 16 = 32 registers
Total in the file     = (L + C) x W + G = 16 x 8 + 8 = 136 registers
Activations held      = W - 1 = 7 before a window-overflow trap
Saved per trap        = L + C = 16 registers = 64 bytes (32-bit registers)

rows: Gates, flip-flops and decoders forming a sequential circuit
A control memory of microinstructions plus a sequencer
Faster; no control-memory read per step
Slower; every step reads a microinstruction
Easy to add as longer microroutines
RISC, and the simple instructions of modern x86
Classic CISC such as the VAX and most IBM System/360 models

concepts.text: Why the RISC recipe suits a pipeline:
items: Fixed length and alignment: the next instruction's address is known during fetch, and one fetch per cycle never straddles two words.
Fixed field positions: register numbers sit in the same bits of every format, so the register file can be read while the opcode is still being decoded.
Load/store only: an arithmetic instruction never waits for memory, and each instruction makes at most one data access, so a single memory stage suffices.
Uniform simple steps: every instruction flows through the same stages instead of variable-length microroutines that stall a CISC pipeline.
Compiler help: the compiler reorders code to fill load-delay and branch-delay slots, so the hardware needs fewer interlocks.

concepts.text: Common mistakes: judging machines by instruction count or by MIPS instead of by execution time; taking the plain mean of class CPIs instead of the frequency-weighted mean; mixing up CPI and IPC (IPC = 1 / CPI); mixing MHz with ns or ms without converting; and using (L + 2C)W + G for the total register count, which counts every overlap twice. Remember also that a window-overflow trap saves only the incoming and local registers of one window.

formulas.plainText: CPU time = IC × CPI × T_clk = IC × CPI / f_clk
Speedup = (IC_CISC × CPI_CISC) / (IC_RISC × CPI_RISC) at equal clock
Total registers with W overlapped windows = (L + C)W + G
Registers visible to one procedure = L + 2C + G

notes.text: Attach one keyword to each side and the comparison table writes itself: CISC = variable length, many modes, microprogrammed, memory-to-memory, few registers; RISC = fixed length, few modes, hardwired, load/store, many registers, CPI about 1.

RISC does not mean a smaller or slower program. The program is longer in instructions but usually faster because CPI is near 1 and the clock is faster; judge with IC × CPI × T_clk, never with instruction count alone.
Berkeley RISC I figures worth remembering: 138 registers, 10 global, 8 windows, 32 registers visible per procedure; window size = 10 + 2 × 6 + 10 = 32.

formulas.title: CPU time
formulas.plainText: T_CPU = IC × CPI × T_clk
formulas.description: Execution time of a program; RISC lowers CPI and T_clk while CISC lowers IC, and only the product matters.

formulas.title: Relative speed at equal clock
formulas.plainText: T1/T2 = (IC1 × CPI1) / (IC2 × CPI2)
formulas.description: Ratio of execution times of two instruction sets running at the same clock frequency.

formulas.title: Register window total
formulas.plainText: N = (L + C) × W + G
formulas.description: Registers in a file with W overlapped windows, L locals and C common registers per window and G globals; Berkeley RISC I: (10 + 6) × 8 + 10 = 138.

flashcards.front: Why is a RISC processor easier to pipeline than a CISC processor?
flashcards.back: All RISC instructions are the same length, take about one cycle and only load/store touch memory, so every instruction passes through identical stages with no variable-length decode or multiple memory accesses to stall the pipeline.

flashcards.front: What is a load/store architecture?
flashcards.back: An instruction set in which only LOAD and STORE instructions access memory; every arithmetic or logical instruction operates on registers. It is a defining feature of RISC.

flashcards.front: What do overlapped register windows achieve?
flashcards.back: Each procedure gets its own window of registers, and neighbouring windows share a few registers in which parameters and results are passed, so a call or return moves a pointer instead of saving registers to memory.

flashcards.front: How do modern x86 processors execute CISC instructions quickly?
flashcards.back: The decoder breaks each x86 instruction into fixed-length micro-ops that a RISC-style pipelined, superscalar core executes; only rare complex instructions use microcode.

questions.questionText: A RISC processor uses overlapped register windows with 10 global registers, 8 windows, 10 local registers per window and 6 registers common to adjacent windows. The total number of registers in the file is:
questions.explanation: N = (L + C)W + G = (10 + 6) × 8 + 10 = 138, the Berkeley RISC I organisation. Each procedure sees L + 2C + G = 32 registers.

questions.questionText: The same program compiles to 0.8 million instructions on a CISC machine (average CPI 3) and to 1.2 million instructions on a RISC machine (average CPI 1.2). Both run at 500 MHz. Which statement is correct?
options: The CISC machine is faster by a factor of 1.5 because it executes fewer instructions
The two machines take the same time
The RISC machine is faster by a factor of about 2.5
The RISC machine is faster by a factor of about 1.67
questions.explanation: T = IC × CPI / f. CISC: 0.8M × 3 / 500M = 4.8 ms; RISC: 1.2M × 1.2 / 500M = 2.88 ms. Ratio 4.8 / 2.88 = 1.67 in favour of RISC despite 50 percent more instructions.

questions.questionText: In a load/store architecture such as MIPS or RISC-V, which instructions are allowed to read or write data memory?
options: Every arithmetic and logic instruction, through memory operands
Only the LOAD and STORE instructions
Any instruction that uses indirect addressing
questions.explanation: In a load/store (RISC) design, ALU instructions work only on registers and immediates; LOAD brings a word from memory into a register and STORE writes it back.

questions.questionText: Three of these instruction-set families are RISC designs. Which one is the CISC design?
questions.explanation: The VAX, with hundreds of instructions, variable-length encoding and many memory addressing modes, is the classic CISC machine; ARM, MIPS and SPARC are RISC designs.

questions.questionText: Which type of control unit is typical of a RISC processor?
options: Microprogrammed control with a writable control store
questions.explanation: Simple, uniform RISC instructions can be decoded by fast combinational logic, so RISC uses hardwired control; microprogramming suits large, complex CISC instruction sets.

questions.questionText: Why is a CISC program for a task usually shorter, in number of instructions, than the RISC program for the same task?
options: CISC compilers delete more instructions during optimisation
A single CISC instruction can do more work, such as fetching memory operands and computing in one step
CISC processors have more registers, so fewer loads are needed
Every CISC instruction is shorter in bytes than every RISC instruction
questions.explanation: Complex instructions with memory operands combine what RISC does with separate loads, ALU operations and stores, so the instruction count IC is lower even though each instruction takes more cycles.

questions.questionText: Which statement about RISC is NOT correct?
options: Most RISC instructions complete at a rate of one per clock cycle in a pipeline
A RISC program always contains fewer instructions than the equivalent CISC program
RISC relies on an optimising compiler for register allocation and instruction scheduling
RISC instructions have a fixed length and few formats
questions.explanation: RISC programs usually contain more instructions than CISC programs, because each instruction does less; RISC wins through a lower CPI and a faster clock, not a lower instruction count.

questions.questionText: How do fixed-length instructions with fixed field positions make a RISC pipeline simpler?
options: They let each instruction access memory several times without stalling
They remove the need for a program counter
The next instruction's address is known during fetch, and register fields sit in the same bits of every format, so registers can be read while the opcode is decoded
They let the processor skip the decode stage entirely
questions.explanation: With every instruction one word long, fetch simply adds the word size to the PC, and fixed register-field positions let register reading overlap decoding, so every instruction passes through the same short stages.

questions.questionText: Studies of compiled high-level-language programs that led to the Berkeley RISC design found which fact that motivated overlapped register windows?
options: Programs rarely used local scalar variables
Procedure calls and returns were the most time-consuming operations, largely because of saving registers and passing parameters
questions.explanation: Weighted by the machine instructions and memory references they cause, calls and returns cost the most, and most operands were local scalars; keeping those in register windows removes most call overhead.

questions.questionText: With overlapped register windows, where does a calling procedure place the parameters for the procedure it calls?
options: In its outgoing (common) registers, which become the callee's incoming registers when the window pointer moves
In the global registers only, which every procedure shares
On the memory stack, because windows cannot share registers
In the callee's local registers, which the caller writes before the call
questions.explanation: Adjacent windows overlap: the caller's outgoing registers are physically the same as the callee's incoming registers, so a call just advances the current-window pointer and no parameter is copied.

questions.questionText: In a circular register file of overlapped windows, what happens when a call is made and no free window is left?
options: A window-overflow trap saves the oldest window's registers to memory so that its window can be reused
The call is refused and the program is aborted
The newest window is overwritten without being saved
The processor switches to microprogrammed mode and uses the memory stack
questions.explanation: The overflow trap spills the oldest activation's window to memory; a later return into that procedure raises an underflow trap that reloads it.

questions.questionText: A register file is organised as a circular buffer of 8 overlapped windows (as in Stallings and SPARC, one window is kept free because the newest window's outgoing registers would otherwise overlap the oldest window's incoming registers). At most how many procedure activations can be held in registers at once before a window-overflow trap is needed?
questions.explanation: The ring closes on itself: the outgoing registers of the newest window would overlap the incoming registers of the oldest, so an N-window file holds N − 1 = 7 activations.

questions.questionText: A register file of 224 registers consists of 8 global registers plus overlapped windows, each window having 12 local registers and 6 registers common with each adjacent window. How many windows does the file have?
questions.explanation: Total = (L + C)W + G, so W = (224 − 8) / (12 + 6) = 216 / 18 = 12. Dividing by L + 2C = 24 would count each overlap twice and give 9.

questions.questionText: With 16 global registers, 8 local registers per window and 8 registers common to each pair of adjacent windows, how many registers can one procedure address at any time?
questions.explanation: Window size = G + L + 2C = 16 + 8 + 2 × 8 = 40: the globals, the locals, the incoming registers shared with the caller and the outgoing registers shared with the callee.

questions.questionText: A designer wants each procedure to see 32 registers, 8 of them global, with the number of local registers equal to the number of common registers shared with each neighbour. If the file has 8 windows, how many physical registers are needed?
questions.explanation: 32 = G + L + 2C = 8 + 3C gives C = L = 8. Total = (L + C)W + G = 16 × 8 + 8 = 136, the SPARC organisation.

questions.questionText: Each window has 10 local registers and 6 registers common with each neighbour, and registers are 32 bits wide. A window-overflow trap stores the local and incoming registers of the oldest window. If a program triggers 25 overflow traps, how many bytes do the traps write to memory?
questions.explanation: Each trap saves L + C = 16 registers × 4 bytes = 64 bytes, so 25 traps write 25 × 64 = 1600 bytes (400 is the count of words, not bytes).

questions.questionText: A program executes 2.5 million instructions with an average CPI of 2 on a processor whose clock period is 0.5 ns. What is its CPU time?
A program's instruction mix is ALU 50% (CPI 1), loads 20% (CPI 4), stores 10% (CPI 3) and branches 20% (CPI 2). What is its average CPI?
questions.explanation: CPI = 0.5 × 1 + 0.2 × 4 + 0.1 × 3 + 0.2 × 2 = 0.5 + 0.8 + 0.3 + 0.4 = 2.0. The plain mean of the class CPIs (2.5) ignores how often each class occurs.

questions.questionText: A processor runs at 800 MHz with an average CPI of 1.6. What is its MIPS rating?
A benchmark performs 60 million floating-point operations and runs in 0.4 s. What is its MFLOPS rating?
questions.explanation: MFLOPS = FP operations / (time × 10^6) = 60 × 10^6 / (0.4 × 10^6) = 150.

questions.questionText: Instruction classes A, B and C need 1, 2 and 3 cycles on a 1 GHz processor. Code sequence 1 executes 6M A, 1M B and 2M C instructions; sequence 2 executes 3M A, 2M B and 2M C. Which statement is correct?
options: Sequence 1 has the higher MIPS rating, but sequence 2 runs faster
Sequence 1 has the higher MIPS rating and also runs faster
Sequence 2 has the higher MIPS rating and runs faster
Both take the same time because they use the same instruction classes
questions.explanation: Sequence 1: 14M cycles = 14 ms for 9M instructions (643 MIPS). Sequence 2: 13M cycles = 13 ms for 7M instructions (538 MIPS). Sequence 2 is faster despite its lower MIPS rating.

questions.questionText: A CISC machine runs a program as 20 million instructions with CPI 4 at 400 MHz. A RISC machine runs the same program as 30 million instructions with CPI 1.25 at 250 MHz. Which statement is correct?
options: The RISC machine is about 2.13 times faster
The RISC machine is about 1.33 times faster
The CISC machine is 1.5 times faster because it executes fewer instructions
Both machines take the same time
questions.explanation: CISC: 20M × 4 / 400 MHz = 0.2 s. RISC: 30M × 1.25 / 250 MHz = 0.15 s. The ratio 0.2 / 0.15 = 1.33 favours RISC; 2.13 compares cycle counts and ignores the different clock rates.

questions.questionText: The RISC version of a program executes 1.4 times as many instructions as the CISC version, whose average CPI is 3.5. Both machines use the same clock. What is the largest average CPI the RISC machine may have and still be at least as fast?
questions.explanation: At equal clock the RISC machine needs 1.4 × IC × CPI_R ≤ IC × 3.5, so CPI_R ≤ 3.5 / 1.4 = 2.5.

questions.questionText: A CISC machine executes a program as 10 million instructions with CPI 3 at 600 MHz. A RISC machine needs 15 million instructions with CPI 1.2 for the same program. What is the minimum RISC clock frequency needed to match the CISC execution time?
questions.explanation: CISC time = 10M × 3 / 600 MHz = 50 ms. The RISC machine needs 15M × 1.2 = 18M cycles in 50 ms, so f = 18 × 10^6 / 0.05 s = 360 MHz.

questions.questionText: A microprogrammed CISC processor executes each machine instruction as an average of 6 microinstructions, each taking one 10 ns clock cycle. What is its MIPS rating?
questions.explanation: Each machine instruction takes 6 × 10 ns = 60 ns, so the rate is 1 / 60 ns = 16.7 × 10^6 instructions per second, i.e. 16.7 MIPS.

questions.questionText: On a RISC machine, loads are 25% of executed instructions and take 3 cycles; every other instruction takes 1 cycle. A better data cache cuts the load time to 2 cycles. What is the overall speedup, with the same instruction count and clock?
questions.explanation: Old CPI = 0.25 × 3 + 0.75 × 1 = 1.5; new CPI = 0.25 × 2 + 0.75 × 1 = 1.25. Speedup = 1.5 / 1.25 = 1.20; 1.5 is only the speedup of the loads themselves.

questions.questionText: A program runs 10 million instructions at CPI 1.2 on a 500 MHz processor. Adding a complex instruction cuts the instruction count by 10% but raises the average CPI to 1.4 at the same clock. What is the new CPU time?
questions.explanation: Old: 10M × 1.2 / 500 MHz = 24 ms. New: 9M × 1.4 / 500 MHz = 25.2 ms, about 5% slower, so the complex instruction does not pay off.

questions.questionText: A program of 8 million instructions takes 12 ms on a 1.5 GHz processor. What is its average CPI?
A load/store machine with three-register ALU instructions (for example ADD R1, R1, R2) computes X = (A + B) × (C + D), with A, B, C, D and X in memory. What is the minimum number of instructions?
questions.explanation: Four LOADs bring A to D into registers, two ADDs and one MUL work on registers, and one STORE writes X: 4 + 3 + 1 = 8, because only LOAD and STORE may touch memory.

questions.questionText: For X = (A + B) × (C + D), a RISC program has 8 fixed 32-bit instructions. A CISC version uses 3 memory-to-memory three-address instructions (ADD T, A, B; ADD X, C, D; MUL X, T, X), each with a 1-byte opcode and three 2-byte addresses. How many times larger is the RISC code in bytes?
questions.explanation: RISC code = 8 × 4 = 32 bytes; CISC code = 3 × (1 + 3 × 2) = 21 bytes. The ratio 32 / 21 = 1.52; 2.67 compares instruction counts rather than bytes.

questions.questionText: A designer's feature list for a new processor contains the four items below. Which one comes from the RISC tradition rather than from classic CISC?
options: Memory-to-memory arithmetic with many addressing modes
A large register file organised as overlapped register windows
questions.explanation: Large windowed register files come from RISC (Berkeley RISC, SPARC). Classic CISC machines have relatively few registers, many addressing modes, variable-length formats and microprogrammed control.

questions.questionText: What is the main advantage of microprogrammed control over hardwired control?
options: It is always faster, because microinstructions are fetched in parallel
It removes the need for any sequencing logic
The instruction set can be changed or extended by rewriting the control memory instead of redesigning the logic
questions.explanation: A microprogrammed unit stores its control signals as microinstructions, so complex instructions are easy to add or correct; the price is speed, because every step reads the control memory.

questions.questionText: Why does a RISC design depend heavily on an optimising compiler?
options: The compiler must translate each instruction into microcode at run time
The compiler must choose among hundreds of complex instructions for each statement
The compiler must keep variables in the large register file and reorder instructions to fill delay slots and avoid pipeline stalls
The compiler must insert memory-to-memory instructions for arithmetic
questions.explanation: RISC hardware stays simple by leaving register allocation and instruction scheduling (including load-delay and branch-delay slots) to the compiler.

questions.questionText: In a pipelined RISC with delayed branches (no annul option), what happens to the instruction immediately after a branch, in the delay slot?
options: It is always executed, whether or not the branch is taken
It is executed only if the branch is not taken
It is discarded and replaced by a bubble
questions.explanation: A delayed branch takes effect one instruction late, so the delay-slot instruction always executes; the compiler places a useful instruction there, or a NOP if none is available.

questions.questionText:
A RISC uses delayed branches with one delay slot (no annulling). What value does this code store in X?
MOV   R1, #5
BR    L            ; unconditional delayed branch
ADD   R1, R1, #3
ADD   R1, R1, #10
L: STORE X, R1
questions.explanation: MOV sets R1 = 5; the ADD #3 in the delay slot executes before the jump takes effect, giving R1 = 8; ADD #10 is skipped, so X = 8.

questions.questionText: Why is the average CPI of a classic CISC processor well above 1?
options: Many instructions access memory several times and run as multi-step microroutines
Its clock period is shorter than that of a RISC processor
It has too many registers to read in one cycle
questions.explanation: A memory-to-memory instruction must fetch several operands and store a result, and a microprogrammed unit spends one cycle per microinstruction, so one instruction takes many cycles.

questions.questionText: Which statement about MIPS as a performance measure is NOT correct?
options: The MIPS rating depends on the instruction mix of the program being run
A machine with a higher MIPS rating always runs a given program faster
MIPS cannot fairly compare machines with different instruction sets
questions.explanation: MIPS ignores how much work each instruction does: a machine or code sequence can execute more, simpler instructions per second and still take longer, so higher MIPS does not guarantee a shorter time.

questions.questionText: A scientific program executes 200 million instructions, 50 million of which are floating-point operations, with an average CPI of 1.5 on a 1 GHz processor. What is its MFLOPS rating?
questions.explanation: Time = 200M × 1.5 / 1 GHz = 0.3 s, so MFLOPS = 50 × 10^6 / (0.3 × 10^6) = 166.7. The MIPS rating would be 200 / 0.3 = 666.7.

questions.questionText: Compared with CISC, which factor of CPU time = IC × CPI × T does a RISC instruction set usually increase?
questions.explanation: Simpler instructions mean more of them per program, so IC rises; RISC then lowers CPI to about 1 and allows a shorter clock period.

questions.questionText: Which pairing of a CPU-time factor with what mainly determines it is correct?
options: Clock cycle time — the compiler and the program's instruction mix
Instruction count — the instruction set architecture and the compiler
Instruction count — the transistor technology alone
Clock cycle time — the number of instructions in the program
questions.explanation: The number of instructions executed depends on the instruction set and on how the compiler translates the program; the clock cycle time is set by hardware technology and organisation.

questions.questionText: How do modern x86 processors achieve RISC-like pipelining while keeping the CISC instruction set?
options: Hardware decoders translate each x86 instruction into simple fixed-length micro-operations that a RISC-style core executes
They execute every x86 instruction in microcode without pipelining
They require programs to be recompiled into ARM code
They restrict x86 programs to instructions that access memory once
questions.explanation: Since the Pentium Pro, x86 front ends crack instructions into micro-ops that a pipelined, superscalar core schedules like RISC instructions; only rare complex instructions fall back to microcode.

questions.questionText: What is the purpose of compressed 16-bit instruction encodings such as ARM Thumb and the RISC-V C extension?
options: To increase the number of addressable registers
To add memory-to-memory arithmetic to RISC
To improve code density, reducing program memory size and instruction-fetch bandwidth
To replace hardwired control with microcode
questions.explanation: Fixed 32-bit RISC instructions waste space; 16-bit encodings of common instructions shrink programs, which matters in embedded systems with small memories and caches.

questions.questionText: Which set of addressing modes is typical of a RISC instruction set?
options: Memory indirect, autoincrement deferred and scaled index with displacement
Direct memory operands for every arithmetic instruction
Register, immediate and register plus displacement
questions.explanation: RISC keeps a few simple modes: register operands, small immediates, and base register plus displacement for LOAD and STORE. The richer memory modes belong to CISC machines such as the VAX.

questions.questionText: Why do RISC processors provide a large number of general-purpose registers?
options: Because microcode needs one register for each microinstruction
Because variable-length instructions need extra registers for decoding
Because a large register file shortens every instruction's opcode
Because only loads and stores reach memory, keeping operands and local variables in registers cuts memory traffic and speeds procedure calls
questions.explanation: In a load/store machine every operand must be in a register before use, so many registers (or register windows) let the compiler keep variables there and avoid loads, stores and register saving at calls.

questions.questionText: A program takes 10 s on machine A and 15 s on machine B. How many times faster is A than B?
questions.explanation: Performance is the reciprocal of execution time, so A is 15 / 10 = 1.5 times as fast as B.

questions.questionText: A superscalar RISC core running at 2 GHz executes 3.6 billion instructions in 1.5 s. What is its average CPI?

A circular register file has 6 overlapped windows and holds at most W − 1 procedure activations. Each overflow trap saves exactly one window and no window is saved in advance. Starting from main with only main's window in use, the program makes 8 nested calls without any return, so 9 activations exist at the deepest point. How many window-overflow traps occur?
questions.explanation: The file holds W − 1 = 5 activations, so activations 6, 7, 8 and 9 each force one trap: 9 − 5 = 4. Assuming all 6 windows usable would wrongly give 3.

questions.questionText: The 'semantic gap' argument used to justify CISC designs refers to:
options: The delay between issuing a load and receiving its data
The difference in speed between registers and main memory
The difference between high-level-language operations and machine instructions, which designers tried to close with complex instructions and many addressing modes
The unused opcode space left in a fixed-length instruction format
questions.explanation: CISC designers argued that instructions resembling high-level statements would simplify compilers and shorten programs; RISC studies showed those instructions were rarely used.

subtopics.title: Pipelining & Parallel Processing
subtopics.subtitle: Flynn's classes, k-stage speedup, arithmetic and instruction pipelines, hazards

concepts.text: Parallel Processing

Parallel processing is any technique that lets a computer perform several operations at the same time to raise throughput, the amount of work completed per unit time. It can be applied at many levels: inside the ALU (bit-parallel adders), between functional units (separate integer, floating-point and shift units working concurrently), between instructions (pipelining and superscalar issue), between data elements (vector and array processors) and between whole processors (multiprocessors and multicomputers). The higher the level, the more hardware is replicated and the more the software must be organised to exploit it.
Levels of parallelism named by the syllabus source:
items: Instruction-level parallelism (ILP): several instructions of one thread in flight at once, via pipelining, superscalar issue and out-of-order execution.
Data-level parallelism (DLP): one instruction applied to many data items, as in SIMD vector units and GPUs.
Thread-level parallelism (TLP): independent threads run on separate cores or hardware threads of an MIMD machine.
Task-level parallelism: whole jobs or processes distributed across processors, typically MIMD multiprocessors or clusters.

rows: One instruction stream, one data stream
One instruction stream, many data streams
Array processors, vector units, GPUs, SSE/NEON
Many instruction streams, one data stream
Largely theoretical; sometimes cited: systolic arrays, fault-tolerant redundant pipelines
Many instruction streams, many data streams

concepts.text: Pipelining

Pipelining decomposes a task into a sequence of sub-operations, each handled by a dedicated segment (stage) separated from the next by a register, so that different tasks occupy different segments at the same time, like cars on an assembly line. A space-time diagram plots segments on the vertical axis against clock cycles on the horizontal axis: in cycle 1 task T1 is in segment 1; in cycle 2 T1 moves to segment 2 while T2 enters segment 1; after k cycles the pipeline is full and one task finishes every cycle. With k segments and n tasks the first task takes k cycles and the remaining n − 1 tasks take one cycle each, so the whole batch takes k + n − 1 cycles.

concepts.plainText: Speedup S = n·t_n / ((k + n − 1)·t_p); as n grows S → k when t_n = k·t_p

concepts.text: Pipeline performance measures (t_p = clock period of the pipeline, t_n = time for one task without pipelining):
items: Speedup S = n t_n / ((k + n − 1) t_p). If each segment takes the same time and t_n = k t_p, this becomes S = nk/(k + n − 1), whose limit for large n is k.
Efficiency E = S/k = n/(k + n − 1), the fraction of the maximum speedup achieved; it approaches 1 as n grows and equals 1/k for a single task.
Throughput H = n/((k + n − 1) t_p) tasks per unit time; ideally 1/t_p, one task per clock.
The clock period t_p is fixed by the slowest segment plus register delay, so unbalanced stages waste time in the faster ones.

concepts.text: Worked example: a 4-segment pipeline processes 100 tasks. Cycles needed = k + n − 1 = 4 + 99 = 103, against 100 × 4 = 400 for the non-pipelined machine. Speedup S = 400/103 ≈ 3.88, efficiency E = 3.88/4 ≈ 0.97, and throughput is 100 tasks in 103 clocks. With only 4 tasks the speedup would be 16/7 ≈ 2.29, which shows why the pipeline is only worth its cost when many tasks flow through it.
Arithmetic and Instruction Pipelines
An arithmetic pipeline splits a long calculation into stages; the standard example is floating-point addition X = A × 2^a plus Y = B × 2^b:
items: Stage 1: compare the exponents a and b by subtraction.
Stage 2: align the mantissas by shifting the smaller-exponent mantissa right by the exponent difference.
Stage 3: add or subtract the aligned mantissas.
Stage 4: normalise the result (shift and adjust the exponent) and round.
Each stage holds its result in a register, so a new pair of operands can enter every clock; vector supercomputers run their add and multiply units this way.

concepts.text: An instruction pipeline overlaps the phases of the instruction cycle; a typical 5-stage RISC pipeline is:
items: IF (fetch): read the instruction at PC from the instruction cache and increment PC.
ID (decode and operand fetch): decode the opcode, read source registers, compute the effective address.
EX (execute): perform the ALU operation or the address arithmetic for a load/store or branch.
MEM (memory): access the data cache for load and store instructions.
WB (write-back): write the result into the destination register.

Mano's four-segment version is FI (fetch instruction), DA (decode and compute address), FO (fetch operand), EX (execute), with a memory conflict between FI and FO removed by separate instruction and data caches.

concepts.text: Pipeline Hazards and Remedies

rows: Two instructions need the same hardware in the same cycle, e.g. one memory for instruction and data
Duplicate resources (Harvard caches, extra ports); stall one instruction
Instruction reads a register before an earlier instruction has written it
Operand forwarding (bypass), hardware interlock stalls, compiler instruction reordering or NOP insertion
Later instruction writes a register that an earlier one still reads (WAR) or writes (WAW); arise with out-of-order execution
Branch changes PC after later instructions have already been fetched
Delayed branch, branch prediction, branch target buffer, prefetching both paths, loop buffer

concepts.text: The remedies trade hardware for lost cycles. Forwarding routes an ALU result straight from the EX/MEM register to the next instruction's ALU input, removing most RAW stalls; a load followed immediately by a use still costs one stall. A delayed branch lets the compiler fill the slot after a branch with a useful instruction that executes whether or not the branch is taken. Branch prediction guesses the outcome (static: backward taken, forward not taken; dynamic: history bits in a branch target buffer) and flushes the pipeline only on a misprediction. Stalls, also called bubbles or interlocks, are the fallback whenever no trick applies.

Vector processing extends pipelining to whole arrays: one vector instruction such as C(1:100) = A(1:100) + B(1:100) streams 100 element pairs through a pipelined adder, replacing a loop of scalar instructions and its overhead, and is implemented with vector registers and multiple memory modules (interleaving) to sustain one operand per clock. An array processor instead uses many identical processing elements under one control unit (SIMD): the attached array processor is a back-end accelerator for a host computer, while the SIMD array processor has each element with its own local memory executing the same broadcast instruction on different data, the ancestor of today's GPUs.
Going Deeper: Pipeline Timing, Stalls and Speedup Limits

Where k + n − 1 comes from: the first task needs k clocks to pass through all k stages (the fill time), and after that the full pipeline delivers one result per clock, so the other n − 1 tasks add n − 1 clocks. The clock cannot be shorter than the slowest stage plus the delay d of the latch (pipeline register) that separates the stages, so τ = max(τ_i) + d. A non-pipelined unit has no latches and needs only the sum of the stage delays per task, so with unequal stages the speedup for very long batches tends to Σ τ_i / τ, which is below k. Pipelining also lengthens the latency of one task to k τ ≥ Σ τ_i; it is the throughput that improves.

concepts.plainText: Clock τ = max(τ_i) + d; batch time T_k = (k + n − 1)·τ; limiting speedup S∞ = (Σ τ_i) / (max τ_i + d)

concepts.text:
Stages 45, 60, 75, 50 ns; latch d = 5 ns; n = 1000 tasks
Clock          τ = max(45, 60, 75, 50) + 5 = 80 ns
Pipelined      T = (4 + 1000 − 1) × 80 = 80 240 ns ≈ 80.24 µs
Non-pipelined  1000 × (45 + 60 + 75 + 50) = 1000 × 230 = 230 000 ns
Speedup        S = 230 000 / 80 240 ≈ 2.87  (limit 230/80 = 2.875, not k = 4)
Efficiency     E = S/k = 2.87/4 ≈ 0.72  (imbalance and latches waste 28%)
Latency        one task: 4 × 80 = 320 ns, against 230 ns unpipelined

Hazards are paid for in stall cycles. With an ideal CPI of 1, each stall adds directly to the average, so CPI_eff = 1 + Σ f_j c_j, where f_j is the fraction of instructions that suffer c_j stall cycles, and for balanced stages the speedup over the unpipelined machine becomes k / CPI_eff. A branch resolved at the end of stage s has s − 1 wrong-path instructions behind it: with predict-not-taken only taken branches pay this penalty, while a pipeline that stalls fetch until every branch resolves pays it on all of them.

5-stage pipeline, ideal CPI = 1, full forwarding, predict-not-taken
Loads     25% of instructions; 40% of them are followed at once by a user
          → 1 load-use stall each: 0.25 × 0.40 × 1 = 0.10 cycles/instr
Branches  20% of instructions; 65% taken; taken penalty 2 cycles
          → 0.20 × 0.65 × 2 = 0.26 cycles/instr
CPI_eff = 1 + 0.10 + 0.26 = 1.36
Speedup over the unpipelined datapath (5 clocks/instr, same clock)
          = 5 / 1.36 ≈ 3.68

Cycle          1    2    3    4    5    6    7    8
LW  R1,0(R2)   IF   ID   EX   MEM  WB
ADD R3,R1,R4        IF   ID   ID   EX   MEM  WB
OR  R7,R8,R9             IF   IF   ID   EX   MEM  WB
Cycle 4: ADD is held in ID, OR is held in IF and a bubble enters EX.
Cycle 5: LW's data in the MEM/WB register is forwarded to ADD's EX.
Total 8 cycles instead of the ideal 5 + 3 − 1 = 7.

A vector instruction on n elements streams through a k-stage pipelined unit in about k + n − 1 clocks, so vector machines hide the fill time by working on long vectors and by chaining the output of one pipelined unit into the next. Memory must keep up: if a module needs m clocks per access, at least m modules are interleaved, with consecutive addresses in consecutive modules, so that one word can be delivered every clock although no single module is any faster. Matrix work shows why this matters: multiplying two n × n matrices takes n^2 inner products of length n, that is n^3 multiply-add operations, 27 for n = 3 and a million for n = 100.

Amdahl's law applies the same reasoning to parallel processors. If a fraction f of the original run time can be spread perfectly over p processors and the remaining 1 − f is serial, the new time is (1 − f) + f/p of the old one. The serial part sets a hard ceiling of 1/(1 − f): a program that is 10% serial can never run more than 10 times faster, and 16 processors give only 1/(0.1 + 0.9/16) = 6.4. Replacing p by the speedup of any enhanced part gives the general form used for vector units and other accelerators.

concepts.plainText: S(p) = 1 / ((1 − f) + f/p); S_max = 1/(1 − f) as p → ∞, where f is the parallelisable fraction of the original time

concepts.text: Common slips in pipeline problems: taking the average stage delay instead of the slowest one for the clock, forgetting the latch delay (or adding it to the non-pipelined time), counting nk or k + n cycles instead of k + n − 1, and quoting a speedup above k, or above Σ τ_i / τ when the stages are unequal. In CPI problems, multiply the branch penalty by the fraction of instructions that actually pay it, for example only taken branches under predict-not-taken.

formulas.plainText: Speedup of a k-stage pipeline on n tasks, S = nk/(k + n − 1)
Maximum speedup as n → ∞ equals the number of stages k
Efficiency E = S/k = n/(k + n − 1)
Throughput H = n / ((k + n − 1) t_p) tasks per unit time
Cycles: k + n − 1 pipelined versus nk non-pipelined

notes.text: For any speedup MCQ compute cycles first: pipelined = k + n − 1, unpipelined = nk (or n t_n / t_p when the times differ), then divide. 4 stages, 100 tasks → 400/103 ≈ 3.88; 5 stages, 200 tasks → 1000/204 ≈ 4.90.
Speedup never exceeds k, and only approaches it for large n. If an option is greater than the number of stages it is wrong, and for a handful of tasks the speedup is far below k.
RAW is the only true data dependency; WAR and WAW are name dependencies that appear only when instructions can complete out of order, and register renaming removes them.
Flynn's MISD class has no widely accepted commercial example; if asked which class is 'rarely or never implemented', the answer is MISD.

formulas.title: Pipeline speedup
formulas.plainText: S = nk / (k + n − 1)
formulas.description: Speedup of a k-segment pipeline processing n tasks when every segment takes one clock; 4 stages and 100 tasks give 3.88.

formulas.title: General speedup
formulas.description: Speedup when a non-pipelined task takes t_n and the pipeline clock is t_p; tends to t_n/t_p for large n.

formulas.title: Pipeline efficiency
formulas.plainText: E = S/k = n / (k + n − 1)
formulas.description: Fraction of the ideal speedup k actually obtained; approaches 1 as the number of tasks grows.

formulas.title: Pipeline throughput
formulas.description: Tasks completed per unit time; the ideal is one task per clock period t_p.

flashcards.front: State Flynn's four classes with one example each.
flashcards.back: SISD: uniprocessor. SIMD: array or vector processor, GPU. MISD: theoretical, no common machine. MIMD: multiprocessor or multicore system.

flashcards.front: How many clock cycles does a k-segment pipeline need for n tasks, and what is the resulting speedup?
flashcards.back: k + n − 1 cycles, against nk without pipelining, so S = nk/(k + n − 1), which approaches k for large n.

flashcards.front: Name the three pipeline hazards and one remedy for each.
flashcards.back: Structural (resource conflict): duplicate the resource or stall. Data (RAW/WAR/WAW): forwarding, interlock stalls, renaming. Control (branches): delayed branch, branch prediction, branch target buffer.

flashcards.front: What are the four stages of a floating-point add pipeline?
flashcards.back: Compare exponents, align mantissas by shifting, add or subtract mantissas, normalise and round the result.

questions.questionText: A 5-segment pipeline in which every segment takes one clock cycle processes 200 tasks. The speedup over a non-pipelined unit performing the same tasks is closest to:
questions.explanation: Pipelined cycles = k + n − 1 = 5 + 199 = 204; non-pipelined = 200 × 5 = 1000. S = 1000/204 ≈ 4.90, just below the ceiling of k = 5.

questions.questionText: In an instruction pipeline, instruction I2 tries to read register R1 before the preceding instruction I1 has written its result into R1. This is a:
questions.explanation: A read that must wait for an earlier write is a read-after-write, or true data, dependency. It is normally cured by operand forwarding or a one-cycle stall.

questions.questionText: Flynn's taxonomy classifies computer architectures according to:
options: The number of processors and the number of memory modules
The number of concurrent instruction streams and data streams
The word length and the clock frequency of the processor
Whether memory is shared by all processors or distributed among them
questions.explanation: Flynn classifies machines by how many instruction streams and how many data streams are processed at the same time, giving SISD, SIMD, MISD and MIMD. Shared versus distributed memory is a later subdivision of MIMD, not Flynn's criterion.

questions.questionText: A quad-core processor in which each core fetches its own instructions and works on its own data belongs to which of Flynn's classes?
questions.explanation: Each core has its own instruction stream and its own data stream, so the machine is multiple-instruction, multiple-data. Multicore CPUs, multiprocessors and clusters are all MIMD.

questions.questionText: According to Mano, a uniprocessor that obtains its parallelism from an instruction pipeline and multiple functional units belongs to which of Flynn's classes?
options: SISD, because there is still one instruction stream operating on one data stream
MIMD, because several instructions are in execution at the same time
SIMD, because one control unit drives all the pipeline stages
MISD, because several stages work on the same data item
questions.explanation: Mano states that an SISD computer may achieve parallel processing by means of multiple functional units or pipeline processing. Overlapping the phases of one instruction stream does not create extra instruction or data streams, so the machine remains SISD.

questions.questionText: Which statement about a SIMD array processor is correct?
options: Each processing element fetches and decodes its own instruction stream from a shared memory
It is a single arithmetic pipeline whose stages work on successive elements of a vector
A master control unit broadcasts each instruction to many processing elements, each with its own local memory, which execute it on different data
All processing elements operate on one shared data item with different instructions
questions.explanation: In Mano's SIMD array processor identical processing elements with local memories execute the same broadcast instruction in lockstep on different data. Independent instruction streams would be MIMD, a single pipeline is a vector processor, and one data item with many instructions is MISD.

questions.questionText: A 6-stage pipeline has a clock period of 5 ns and no stalls. How long does it take to complete 50 tasks?
questions.explanation: T = (k + n − 1)τ = (6 + 50 − 1) × 5 ns = 55 × 5 = 275 ns. 1500 ns is the non-pipelined time (50 × 6 × 5 ns), 250 ns forgets the k − 1 fill cycles and 55 is the number of clock cycles, not the time.

questions.questionText: In the space-time diagram of a 4-segment pipeline (one clock per segment, no stalls), task T1 enters segment 1 in clock cycle 1. In which clock cycle does task T6 complete segment 4?
