questions.explanation: Task Ti enters segment 1 in cycle i and leaves segment k in cycle i + k − 1, so T6 finishes in cycle 6 + 4 − 1 = 9. Cycle 24 would be the non-pipelined finish (6 × 4).

questions.questionText: A 5-stage pipeline with equal stage delays processes 20 tasks without stalls. What is its efficiency (the fraction of the ideal speedup k that is achieved)?
questions.explanation: E = n/(k + n − 1) = 20/24 ≈ 0.833, equivalently S/k with S = 100/24 ≈ 4.17. 0.800 comes from using k + n instead of k + n − 1, and 4.17 is the speedup itself.

questions.questionText: A 5-stage pipeline with a 4 ns clock processes a batch of 10 tasks with no stalls. What is the throughput measured over the whole batch?
questions.explanation: Time = (5 + 10 − 1) × 4 ns = 56 ns, so H = 10/56 ns ≈ 178.6 × 10^6 tasks/s. 250 million is the ideal 1/τ reached only for very long batches, 50 million is the non-pipelined rate 1/(5 × 4 ns) and 166.7 million counts k + n cycles.

questions.questionText: The four stages of a pipeline have delays of 40, 30, 60 and 50 ns, and each interstage latch adds 10 ns. What is the minimum clock period?
questions.explanation: τ = max(τ_i) + d = 60 + 10 = 70 ns. 60 ns forgets the latch, 55 ns uses the average stage delay (45 + 10) and 190 ns adds a single latch delay to the sum of the four stage delays (180 + 10).

questions.questionText: A non-pipelined unit takes 100 ns per instruction. It is split into 4 stages with delays of 20, 25, 30 and 25 ns, and a 5 ns latch is added after each stage. Ignoring hazards, what speedup does the pipeline give for 200 instructions?
questions.explanation: τ = 30 + 5 = 35 ns; pipelined time = (4 + 199) × 35 = 7105 ns; non-pipelined time = 200 × 100 = 20 000 ns; S = 20 000/7105 ≈ 2.82. Ignoring the latch gives 3.28, and the equal-stage formula nk/(k + n − 1) gives 3.94.

questions.questionText: A task needs 40 ns in a non-pipelined unit that has no latches. In a 4-stage pipeline the stage delays are 10, 8, 12 and 10 ns and each latch adds 2 ns. What is the maximum speedup obtainable for a very long stream of tasks?
questions.explanation: τ = 12 + 2 = 14 ns, and for n → ∞ the speedup tends to t_n/τ = 40/14 ≈ 2.86. 3.33 forgets the latch (40/12), 3.43 wrongly adds four latch delays to the non-pipelined time (48/14), and 4 holds only for balanced stages with no latch overhead.

questions.questionText: A four-segment floating-point adder pipeline has segment delays of 60, 70, 100 and 80 ns and interface registers with a 10 ns delay. How long does it take to add 100 pairs of numbers, with no stalls?
questions.explanation: τ = 100 + 10 = 110 ns; T = (4 + 100 − 1) × 110 ns = 103 × 110 = 11 330 ns ≈ 11.33 µs. 31.0 µs is the non-pipelined time 100 × (60 + 70 + 100 + 80) ns, 10.30 µs forgets the register delay and 11.00 µs forgets the fill cycles.

questions.questionText: A 5-stage pipeline has stage delays of 20, 25, 20, 30 and 25 ns and a 5 ns latch after each stage. The non-pipelined unit takes 120 ns per instruction. When the pipeline is clocked at its minimum clock period, what is the latency of a single instruction in it?
questions.explanation: Every stage occupies one full clock τ = 30 + 5 = 35 ns, so an instruction needs kτ = 5 × 35 = 175 ns from entry to exit: pipelining raises latency while it improves throughput. 145 ns adds the latches to the raw delays but ignores that each stage must wait for the whole clock, and 35 ns is the clock period.

questions.questionText: A non-pipelined processor takes 50 ns per instruction. It is pipelined either into 5 or into 10 equal stages, and each latch adds 2 ns. For a very long instruction stream with no hazards, how many times faster is the 10-stage design than the 5-stage design?
questions.explanation: 5 stages: τ = 50/5 + 2 = 12 ns; 10 stages: τ = 50/10 + 2 = 7 ns. For a long stream the time per instruction is τ, so the ratio is 12/7 ≈ 1.71, not 2, because the latch overhead does not shrink. 7.14 is the 10-stage speedup over the non-pipelined processor (50/7) and 0.58 inverts the ratio.

questions.questionText: A 5-stage pipeline with equal stages and no stalls must reach a speedup of at least 4 over the non-pipelined unit. What is the minimum number of tasks n in the batch?
A 4-stage pipeline with equal stages and a 20 ns clock processes 36 tasks without stalls. What are its efficiency and its throughput?
questions.explanation: Cycles = 4 + 36 − 1 = 39. E = n/(k + n − 1) = 36/39 ≈ 0.923 and H = 36/(39 × 20 ns) = 36/780 ns ≈ 46.2 × 10^6 tasks/s. 50.0 million is the ideal 1/τ, the 0.900 and 45.0 pair counts k + n = 40 cycles, and 0.250 and 12.5 million are non-pipelined figures.

questions.questionText: Which of the following is NOT a reason why the actual speedup of a k-stage pipeline is less than k?
options: The k − 1 cycles needed to fill the pipeline
Using separate instruction and data caches
Unequal stage delays, since the clock must suit the slowest stage
The delay of the latches between stages
questions.explanation: Fill time, stage imbalance and latch overhead all pull the speedup below k. Separate instruction and data caches remove a structural hazard, so they help the pipeline approach its ideal rather than limiting it.

questions.questionText: Pipelining an instruction unit mainly improves:
options: Throughput: more instructions are completed per unit time, although the latency of each instruction is not reduced
The latency of each individual instruction, which becomes k times shorter
The number of instructions in the program, which decreases
The hit ratio of the instruction cache
questions.explanation: Overlapping instructions raises the completion rate towards one per clock, but each instruction still passes through all k stages, and the latch overhead makes its latency slightly longer than before.

questions.questionText: Which statement about the registers (latches) placed between pipeline stages is correct?
options: They shorten the latency of a single task by storing partial results
They are needed only in arithmetic pipelines, not in instruction pipelines
They remove all data hazards because every result is stored in them
They hold each stage's result for the next stage, so every stage can work on a different task in the same clock, but their delay is added to the clock period
questions.explanation: Pipeline registers isolate the stages so that k tasks can be in progress at once; the price is the latch delay d in τ = max τ_i + d. Data hazards still need forwarding or stalls even though results pass through the latches.

questions.questionText: In a four-segment floating-point adder pipeline, which segment shifts the mantissa of the number with the smaller exponent to the right?
options: Segment 3: add or subtract the mantissas
questions.explanation: Segment 1 subtracts the exponents to find their difference, segment 2 shifts the smaller-exponent mantissa right by that difference, segment 3 adds the aligned mantissas and segment 4 normalises the result.

questions.questionText: In the classic 5-stage RISC pipeline IF–ID–EX–MEM–WB, in which stage does a load instruction read the data cache?
questions.explanation: EX computes the effective address, MEM reads the data cache at that address and WB writes the loaded value into the destination register. IF reads the instruction cache, not the data cache.

questions.questionText: In Mano's four-segment instruction pipeline (FI, DA, FO, EX), if there is only one memory, which two segments can need memory in the same clock cycle and so conflict?
questions.explanation: FI fetches a new instruction while FO of an earlier instruction fetches its operand from memory, so both need memory at once. Mano notes that separate instruction and data memories remove this conflict.

questions.questionText: In Mano's three-segment RISC pipeline (I: instruction fetch, A: ALU operation, E: execute), what does the delayed-load technique do?
options: The compiler places a no-operation, or an independent instruction, after a load whose result is needed by the next instruction, instead of relying on a hardware interlock
The hardware delays every load by one extra cycle so that the data cache can be refreshed
The compiler moves the load after the instruction that uses its result
The processor fetches the operands of two loads in the same cycle
questions.explanation: In Mano's RISC pipeline a loaded value is not yet available to the very next instruction, so the compiler detects the conflict and inserts a no-op (or schedules an unrelated instruction) in that slot; this software solution is called delayed load.

questions.questionText: A conditional branch is not resolved until the EX stage, but the instructions that follow it have already been fetched. The resulting problem is a:
questions.explanation: A control hazard arises when the PC changes after instructions on the wrong path have already entered the pipeline; they must be flushed, or the branch handled by prediction or delayed branching.

questions.questionText:
For the instruction sequence below, which list of dependences is complete and correct?

I1: LOAD R1, 0(R2)
I2: ADD  R3, R1, R4
I3: SUB  R1, R5, R6
options: RAW I1→I2 on R1; WAR I2→I3 on R1; WAW I1→I3 on R1
RAW I1→I2 on R1; RAW I2→I3 on R1; WAW I1→I3 on R1
WAR I1→I2 on R1; RAW I2→I3 on R1; WAW I1→I3 on R1
questions.explanation: I2 reads R1 written by I1 (RAW), I3 writes R1 that I2 reads (WAR), and I1 and I3 both write R1 (WAW). No other register is shared: R3 is written by I2 and not used again.

questions.questionText: In a simple in-order 5-stage pipeline where operands are read only in ID and results are written only in WB, which data hazards can occur?
options: RAW, WAR and WAW can all occur
Only RAW; WAR and WAW cannot occur because reads and writes happen in fixed stages in program order
Only WAW, because two instructions can write the same register
Only WAR, because a later instruction may write before an earlier one reads
questions.explanation: Every instruction reads its operands in ID before any later instruction reaches WB, and writes happen in program order in WB, so only true (RAW) dependences cause hazards. WAR and WAW hazards appear with out-of-order completion, for example with long floating-point pipelines.

questions.questionText:
A 5-stage pipeline (IF, ID, EX, MEM, WB) has no forwarding; the register file is written in the first half of a clock and read in the second half, and the hazard is handled by stalling the dependent instruction in ID. How many stall cycles occur between the two instructions below?

ADD R1, R2, R3
SUB R4, R1, R5
questions.explanation: ADD writes R1 in WB in cycle 5, so SUB can read R1 in ID no earlier than cycle 5 instead of cycle 3: 2 stall cycles. Forwarding from the EX/MEM register would remove them.

questions.questionText:
A 5-stage pipeline (IF, ID, EX, MEM, WB) has full forwarding and a hazard-detection unit, and there are no other stalls. How many clock cycles are needed for the sequence below, from the first IF to the last WB?

LW  R1, 0(R2)
ADD R3, R1, R4
SUB R5, R3, R6
questions.explanation: The ideal time is 5 + 3 − 1 = 7 cycles. The load-use dependence LW→ADD costs one stall because the loaded value is ready only after MEM, while ADD→SUB is covered by forwarding with no stall, giving 8 cycles (11 without forwarding).

questions.questionText:
A 5-stage pipeline (IF, ID, EX, MEM, WB) has no forwarding; the register file is written in the first half and read in the second half of a clock, and hazards are handled by stalling in ID. How many cycles does the sequence take, from the first IF to the last WB?

I1: ADD R1, R2, R3
I2: SUB R4, R1, R5
I3: AND R6, R1, R7
I4: OR  R8, R4, R6
questions.explanation: I1 writes R1 in cycle 5, so I2 reads it then and executes in cycle 6 (2 stalls); R1 is then ready for I3, which executes in cycle 7 and writes R6 in cycle 9. I4 must read R6 in cycle 9 and executes in cycle 10 (2 more stalls), so its WB is in cycle 12, against 8 cycles with no hazards.

questions.questionText: Operand forwarding (bypassing) removes many RAW stalls by:
options: Writing every result to memory so that later instructions can load it
Having the compiler insert no-operation instructions between dependent instructions
Routing a result from a pipeline register straight to the ALU input of a following instruction before it is written to the register file
Predicting the value that the earlier instruction will produce
questions.explanation: Forwarding adds multiplexers at the ALU inputs fed from the EX/MEM and MEM/WB registers, so a result can be used in the very next cycle instead of waiting for write-back. Inserting no-ops is a software remedy that keeps the lost cycles rather than removing them.

questions.questionText: Why does a load followed immediately by an instruction that uses the loaded register still need one stall cycle in a 5-stage pipeline with full forwarding?
options: The register file cannot be read and written in the same cycle
The loaded data is available only at the end of MEM, but the dependent instruction needs it at the start of its EX in that same cycle
Loads use the instruction cache, which causes a structural hazard
The branch predictor must first check the address of the load
questions.explanation: An ALU result exists at the end of EX, one cycle before the next instruction's EX, so it can be forwarded; a load result exists only after MEM, which coincides with the next instruction's EX, so one bubble is unavoidable unless the compiler schedules an independent instruction there.

questions.questionText: In a pipeline with an ideal CPI of 1, 20% of the instructions are branches and every branch causes a 2-cycle stall. What is the effective CPI?
questions.explanation: CPI = 1 + f_branch × penalty = 1 + 0.20 × 2 = 1.4. 1.2 uses a 1-cycle penalty, 1.6 wrongly counts 3 cycles per branch and 3.0 adds the full penalty to every instruction.

questions.questionText: A 5-stage pipeline with an ideal CPI of 1 uses predict-not-taken. 25% of instructions are branches and 60% of branches are taken; each taken branch costs 3 cycles, not-taken branches cost nothing, and there are no other stalls. What is its speedup over a non-pipelined version of the same datapath that takes 5 clock cycles per instruction at the same clock?
questions.explanation: CPI = 1 + 0.25 × 0.60 × 3 = 1.45, so S = 5/1.45 ≈ 3.45. Penalising every branch gives CPI 1.75 and S = 2.86; penalising the not-taken branches instead (0.40) gives CPI 1.30 and S = 3.85.

questions.questionText: In Stallings' six-stage instruction pipeline (FI, DI, CO, FO, EI, WO), a conditional branch is resolved at the end of its EI stage and turns out to be taken. With no branch prediction, how many instructions fetched after the branch must be discarded?
questions.explanation: While the branch moves from FI to the end of EI, the four following instructions enter FI, DI, CO and FO behind it; all four are on the wrong path and are flushed, a penalty of 4 cycles (Stallings' example: a branch at I3 to I15 discards I4 to I7).

questions.questionText: Which technique for dealing with conditional branches keeps a small, very fast memory of the most recently fetched instructions in sequence, so that a short loop can be executed again without fetching from memory?
questions.explanation: Stallings lists multiple streams, prefetch of the branch target, the loop buffer, branch prediction and delayed branch. The loop buffer holds the last few sequential instructions, so a backward branch to a target inside it is served from the buffer; a branch target buffer instead stores branch addresses with their targets and prediction bits.

questions.questionText: A loop-closing branch is taken 9 times and then not taken once each time the loop runs, and the loop is run many times. In steady state, how many mispredictions per run of the loop does a 1-bit predictor make, and how many does a 2-bit saturating-counter predictor make?
questions.explanation: The 1-bit predictor misses at the loop exit and again at the first branch of the next run, because the exit flipped its bit. The 2-bit counter only drops from strongly to weakly taken at the exit and still predicts taken on re-entry, so it misses once per run.

questions.questionText: What is stored in a branch target buffer (BTB)?
options: The instructions placed in the delay slots of all branches
Both the taken and not-taken paths of every branch in the program
The addresses of recently executed branch instructions together with their target addresses and prediction history
The return addresses of subroutine calls saved on the stack
questions.explanation: The BTB is a small associative memory looked up with the address of the instruction being fetched; on a hit the predicted target is fetched at once, so a correctly predicted taken branch costs no cycles.

questions.questionText: A pipeline with an ideal CPI of 1 has a single unified memory port. 30% of instructions are loads or stores, and each data access stalls instruction fetch for 1 cycle. How many times faster is the same pipeline with separate instruction and data caches, at the same clock?
questions.explanation: With one port CPI = 1 + 0.30 × 1 = 1.30; with split caches the structural hazard disappears and CPI = 1, so the split design is 1.30/1 = 1.30 times faster. 1.43 misuses 1/(1 − 0.3) and 0.77 inverts the ratio.

questions.questionText: A pipelined processor runs at 800 MHz and, because of stalls, its effective CPI is 1.6. What is its instruction throughput?
questions.explanation: Throughput = f/CPI = 800 × 10^6/1.6 = 500 × 10^6 instructions per second = 500 MIPS. 800 MIPS is the stall-free ideal and 1280 MIPS multiplies by the CPI instead of dividing.

questions.questionText: Why do vector processors use interleaved main memory?
options: So that the vector instruction can be decoded while memory is idle
To keep instructions and data in separate memories and so avoid structural hazards
To reduce the access time of each individual memory module
So that consecutive elements lie in different modules whose accesses overlap, letting memory deliver about one operand per clock to the pipeline
questions.explanation: Interleaving does not make any module faster; with m modules on consecutive addresses, m accesses proceed in parallel and a new word can be delivered every clock once the stream is under way.

questions.questionText: A vector pipeline needs one operand every 10 ns, and each memory module has a cycle time of 80 ns. With consecutive elements in consecutive modules (low-order interleaving), what is the minimum number of modules?
questions.explanation: Each module can start a new access only every 80 ns, so 80/10 = 8 modules working in rotation are needed to deliver one word every 10 ns.

questions.questionText: How many multiply-add operations are needed to multiply two 20 × 20 matrices?
questions.explanation: The product has n^2 = 400 elements, each an inner product of n = 20 terms, so n^3 = 20^3 = 8000 multiply-add operations are needed. 400 counts only the inner products, 16 000 counts the multiplications and additions separately and 7600 counts only the additions.

questions.questionText: 90% of a program's execution time can be parallelised perfectly and the rest is serial. According to Amdahl's law, what speedup is obtained on 10 processors?
